modules.description: Understand what runs where, and put a deliberate colour at a deliberate place.

lessons.intro: A fragment shader is one small function, and the GPU runs a separate copy of it for every single pixel on screen. Your job is to return one colour. You never loop over pixels and you never know which pixel you are, except through the coordinate handed to you. That constraint is what makes shaders fast, and what makes them feel strange at first.

stages.body: The simplest possible shader ignores position entirely and returns the same colour for every pixel. This still runs once per pixel — hundreds of thousands of times for a phone screen — it just happens to produce the same answer each time. fragColor is what you assign to, and its four components are red, green, blue and alpha, each running from zero to one rather than zero to 255.
stages.title: One colour, everywhere

stages.body: fragCoord tells you which pixel this copy of the function is responsible for, measured in pixels from the bottom-left corner. Feeding it into red makes position visible as a gradient. But notice the divisor: four hundred is a guess. On a narrower screen the gradient finishes early, and on a wider one it never reaches full brightness. The coordinate is real, but the scale is arbitrary.
stages.source: fragColor = vec4(fragCoord.x / 400.0, 0.28, 0.22, 1.0);
stages.title: Where am I? Raw pixels

stages.body: iResolution holds the size of the surface being drawn, so dividing fragCoord by it converts pixels into a fraction of the way across. Now zero is the left edge and one is the right edge on every device, and the guess is gone. This normalised coordinate is conventionally called uv, and almost everything else in this course starts from it. Elsewhere you will see it called u_resolution, declared as a vec2.
stages.source:
vec2 uv = fragCoord / iResolution.xy;
fragColor = vec4(uv.x, 0.28, 0.22, 1.0);
stages.title: Divide by the resolution

stages.body: Feeding uv.x into red and uv.y into green makes both axes visible in one image, and gives you a permanently useful debugging tool: when coordinates misbehave, render them as colour and look. Bottom-left is a dark navy rather than black: red and green are both zero there, but the fixed blue stays at 0.22. Top-right is yellow because red and green are both at full. Any corner that surprises you means your coordinates are not what you assumed.
stages.source:
vec2 uv = fragCoord / iResolution.xy;
fragColor = vec4(uv.x, uv.y, 0.22, 1.0);
stages.title: Both axes at once

lessons.takeaway: One function, run once per pixel, returning a colour. You never loop and you never know which pixel you are, except through the coordinate handed to you. Divide that coordinate by the resolution to get a number meaning the same thing on every screen.
lessons.title: What a fragment shader is
lessons.tryThis: Swap uv.x and uv.y in the last stage. Which two corners trade colours, and which two stay put?

lessons.intro: Lesson 1 divided fragCoord by iResolution.xy without asking what either side of that division actually contains. This lesson slows down on that one line: which corner of the screen is (0, 0), why iResolution is a vec3 instead of a vec2, and why uv survives a phone rotating from portrait to landscape when a raw pixel count does not. It also flags a naming mismatch you will meet immediately outside this app: plenty of shader code calls this uniform u_resolution and declares it as a vec2.

stages.body: Green here is driven only by uv.y, so watch it rather than the fixed red and blue. At the bottom of the screen it renders a dark purple — red and blue sit at their fixed 0.12 and 0.35, and green is pinned at zero there — and it climbs to a bright green as uv.y approaches one and green overtakes the other two channels. That tells you where (0, 0) lives: fragCoord, and therefore uv, starts at the bottom-left corner and grows upward and rightward. Many UI frameworks and image formats put the origin at the top-left instead, with y growing downward, so a gradient ported from one of those without adjustment renders upside down here even though every number in it is unchanged.
stages.source:
vec2 uv = fragCoord / iResolution.xy;
fragColor = vec4(0.12, uv.y, 0.35, 1.0);
stages.title: Which corner is home

stages.body: iResolution is a vec3, not the vec2 you might expect from 'a width and a height'. Its .xy holds the real pixel dimensions you already divide by; .z is the pixel aspect ratio, a Shadertoy convention for hardware whose pixels are not square, and it is always 1.0 in this sandbox. Subtracting 1.0 from it leaves blue permanently at zero here, proving the point: on a platform where pixels really were non-square, that same line would shift blue away from zero. Because iResolution is a vec3, dividing a vec2 like fragCoord by the whole thing rather than by iResolution.xy is not just wrong, it does not compile at all.
stages.title: iResolution.xy versus iResolution.z

stages.body: This diagonal blend runs from a dark navy blue in the bottom-left corner to a bright, pale yellow in the top-right, because uv.x and uv.y are each already a fraction from 0 to 1 of their own axis before they are added and halved; the fixed 0.4 in blue is what keeps either corner from reading as pure black or pure white. Rotate the phone from portrait to landscape and iResolution.xy swaps its width and height, but the corners stay the corners: bottom-left is still 0, top-right is still 1, so the image reflows correctly without the shader being recompiled. Compare that with Lesson 1's raw fragCoord.x / 400.0: that divisor was a guess baked into the shader, so the same rotation would change how far across the screen the gradient reaches, sometimes clipping to solid colour before the edge.
stages.title: A gradient that survives rotation

stages.body: Plenty of shader code you will read outside this app, including tutorials like The Book of Shaders, declares this uniform as u_resolution and gives it type vec2 rather than vec3. Their normalising line often reads gl_FragCoord.xy / u_resolution.xy, where the trailing .xy is a harmless no-op swizzle on an already-two-component value. Paste that convention into this sandbox unchanged and it fails: u_resolution does not exist here, and iResolution cannot stand in for it directly because iResolution is a vec3. Anywhere their code uses the bare uniform expecting two components, you must write iResolution.xy explicitly, the same swizzle Lesson 1 introduced, now doing double duty as a translation between naming conventions.
stages.source:
vec2 uv = fragCoord / iResolution.xy;
fragColor = vec4(uv.x, uv.y, 0.5, 1.0);
stages.title: The same idea, other names

lessons.takeaway: iResolution is a vec3 whose .xy holds real pixel width and height; dividing fragCoord by it, not by a guessed number, is what lets a gradient survive resizing or rotation. Elsewhere the same uniform is often called u_resolution and declared as a vec2, so code written against it needs .xy appended wherever it appears here.
lessons.title: From pixels to UV
lessons.tryThis: Remove the .xy from the divisor in the last stage and read the compile error. What type mismatch is the driver complaining about?

lessons.intro: Every stage so far has measured position from a corner, which makes distance from the middle of the screen awkward to express and makes anything meant to look round secretly depend on the screen's proportions. This lesson remaps uv from a 0 to 1 range into a −1 to 1 range centred on the middle of the screen, then confronts the cost of treating a non-square screen as if it were square: a shape meant to be round comes out stretched. length() appears here strictly as a ruler, to measure that stretch, not to draw a shape.

stages.body: Doubling uv and subtracting one turns a 0-to-1 range into a −1-to-1 range: at the exact centre of the screen p is (0, 0); it is negative toward the bottom and left, positive toward the top and right. Watch closely what actually renders, because clamping hits each quadrant differently, not each half. Only where both p.x and p.y are negative — the bottom-left quadrant — do red and green both clamp to zero, leaving a flat dark navy blue, (0, 0, 0.5). The top-left quadrant still shows green climbing as p.y rises above zero, even though red sits pinned at zero there because p.x is negative; the bottom-right quadrant mirrors that, red climbing while green stays pinned at zero. p really is negative everywhere the maths says so — but the framebuffer clamps each colour channel to zero independently, so a region only goes completely still once both of its channels are negative at once.
stages.title: Remap to centred coordinates

stages.body: length(p) here is used purely as a ruler — it measures how far a point is from the centre, it does not draw a shape, and Module 1 has no shape functions yet. On a square screen the resulting grey gradient's contours look like circles. On a real phone screen, which is taller than it is wide, they do not: p.x and p.y are each normalised against a different physical dimension, width for one axis and height for the other, so a fixed step in p covers more real pixels along the wider dimension than the narrower one. The contours you are looking at are ellipses, stretched along whichever screen dimension is larger, even though the code that produced them never mentions an ellipse.
stages.title: A circle-ish gradient, until you check

stages.body: One new line fixes the ellipse from the previous stage: multiplying p.x by iResolution.x / iResolution.y stretches the x axis by exactly the screen's width-to-height ratio before length() ever measures it. length() is still only a ruler here, not a shape — the correction changes what unit the ruler is marked in, not what it draws. On a screen taller than it is wide that ratio is less than one, so p.x is compressed rather than expanded, matching how much less physical width there is to work with per unit of p compared to height. The grey gradient's contours now read as genuine circles, the same on a phone in portrait or landscape.
stages.title: Fix it: scale x by the aspect ratio

stages.body: This is stage one's colour-coded render again, with the same aspect correction from the previous stage applied. Compare the two: the aspect fix reshapes how quickly colour changes as you move away from the middle, but it does not move the middle itself. At the exact centre pixel, uv is (0.5, 0.5), so p starts as (0, 0) before the correction ever runs, and multiplying zero by any aspect ratio is still zero. That is the property worth confirming: aspect correction changes the surrounding falloff, never the origin. Anything you build on top of p — a ring, a stripe, a pattern radiating outward — can rely on the centre staying exactly where it was.
stages.title: Confirm the centre is (0, 0)

lessons.takeaway: Doubling uv and subtracting one centres the origin on the middle of the screen instead of a corner. On a non-square screen that origin is still correct, but a length()-based radial gradient is elliptical until x is scaled by iResolution.x / iResolution.y, after which the same measurement reads as a true circle centred at exactly (0, 0).
lessons.title: Centre and aspect
lessons.tryThis: Try dividing p.y by the aspect ratio instead of multiplying p.x. Does the circle still come out round, and where does it sit on screen?

lessons.intro: Every stage in this course so far has rendered one still frame; this lesson introduces the one uniform that changes on its own without any input from the learner. iTime counts seconds since the sandbox started, and feeding it into colour is deceptively easy to get wrong: used directly it only ever grows, so a naive shader gets brighter forever and then sits stuck at white. This lesson works through turning that endless ramp into a genuinely bounded, controllable animation, and explains why counting seconds rather than counting frames is what keeps the result looking identical on every screen.

stages.body: iTime is seconds since the sandbox started, and it never resets or wraps — it just keeps counting up for as long as this screen stays open. Feeding it straight into every colour channel makes the whole frame start black and get linearly brighter, reaching pure white after about ten seconds. After that it stays white, not because the maths stopped — iTime keeps climbing — but because the screen can only display values from 0 to 1, and anything above 1 clamps to the same white as exactly 1. This is the trap with using iTime directly: it is unbounded, so anything meant to animate indefinitely needs a bounded function of it, not iTime itself.
stages.source:
float brightness = iTime * 0.1;
fragColor = vec4(brightness, brightness, brightness, 1.0);
stages.title: iTime, driven straight into colour

stages.body: sin(iTime) oscillates between −1 and 1 forever, no matter how large iTime grows, which is exactly the bounded behaviour the previous stage lacked. Multiplying by 0.5 and adding 0.5 is the same remap Lesson 3 used in reverse to build p from uv; here it takes sin's −1-to-1 output and lands it inside the 0-to-1 range colour channels actually need, instead of clipping the negative half to black the way an unmapped signal would. A full cycle — dark, bright, dark again — takes about 6.28 seconds, because iTime is measured in the same units sin already expects: radians' worth of seconds, not degrees or an arbitrary frame count.
stages.source:
float brightness = sin(iTime) * 0.5 + 0.5;
fragColor = vec4(brightness, brightness, brightness, 1.0);
stages.title: sin(iTime): bounded, not straight-line

stages.body: Multiplying inside sin's argument compresses time itself before the wave ever sees it: at 3.0, the shader lives through three seconds of oscillation for every one second of iTime, so a cycle that took 6.28 seconds now takes about 2.09. Compare that with multiplying the brightness value sin produces afterward, outside the function — that would change how bright the peaks and troughs are, not how often they occur. Confusing those two multiplications is an easy mistake to make because both are innocuous-looking * operators sitting near sin, but one scales speed and the other scales contrast, and only one of them is what 'faster' actually means here.
stages.source:
float brightness = sin(iTime * 3.0) * 0.5 + 0.5;
fragColor = vec4(brightness, brightness, brightness, 1.0);
stages.title: Change speed: multiply the input, not the output

stages.body: iTime measures wall-clock seconds, not how many frames have been drawn, and that distinction matters the moment two devices differ. A shader that instead incremented a counter once per rendered frame would animate twice as fast on a 120Hz screen as on a 60Hz one, running the identical code, and would visibly stutter if either device dropped frames under load. Because this blue channel is driven by sin(iTime * 2.0), the oscillation takes the same real-world duration everywhere the sandbox runs, regardless of frame rate. You will also meet u_time, used by the same convention as u_resolution, and iGlobalTime, an older Shadertoy uniform iTime replaced — both name the identical idea of elapsed seconds.
stages.title: Elapsed seconds, not a frame count

lessons.takeaway: iTime only ever increases, so feeding it straight into colour saturates and sticks. Wrapping it in sin() turns it into a bounded, repeating signal, and multiplying the argument to sin() — not the result — changes how fast that cycle repeats. Elapsed seconds, not a per-frame counter, is what keeps motion the same speed on a 60Hz and a 120Hz screen.
lessons.title: Time as an input
lessons.tryThis: Change the multiplier in the last stage to a negative number. Which direction does the oscillation reverse, and does the period change?

lessons.intro: Every previous lesson taught maths; this one teaches the tooling around it, because the sandbox has been quietly hiding four things from you since Lesson 1: a precision declaration, two uniform declarations, and the main() that actually runs. That hiding is deliberate scaffolding, not the whole truth, and a learner who copies a body from this app into a bare WebGL page or pastes foreign shader code in here without knowing what changed will hit confusing compile errors. This lesson walks the body you write, the complete program it becomes, the same idea under different uniform names, and what changes if the target is GLSL ES 3.00 instead of 1.00.

stages.body: This body is nothing new: it is Lesson 3's aspect-corrected centring, remapped back into 0-to-1 so it displays as colour instead of clamping away its negative half. What matters this lesson is not the maths but the shape of the file — four lines, no precision line, no uniform declarations, no function signature, no main(), and definitely no gl_FragColor. Every stage in every lesson you have read so far has been exactly this: the inside of one function, handed to a sandbox that supplies everything around it. The next stage names precisely what that surrounding scaffolding contains and why it exists.
stages.title: The body you write

stages.body: Here is the complete program your body actually becomes, exactly as docs/data/shader-sandbox.md describes it: precision highp float; uniform vec3 iResolution; uniform float iTime; void mainImage(out vec4 fragColor, in vec2 fragCoord) { — your lines land here, unindented in the real file — } void main() { vec4 shadercraftColor = vec4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0); mainImage(shadercraftColor, gl_FragCoord.xy); gl_FragColor = shadercraftColor; }. The precision line tells the GPU how much floating-point accuracy to spend; the two uniform lines are the only two values that exist beyond what you compute yourself; mainImage is the function every stage's source has secretly been the body of all along; and main() is what a GLSL program must define to run at all, calling your body through a local variable before writing the result to the built-in gl_FragColor, because passing that built-in straight through as an out parameter is rejected by some drivers.
stages.source:
vec2 uv = fragCoord / iResolution.xy;
fragColor = vec4(uv.x, uv.y, 0.5, 1.0);
stages.title: The whole program it compiles into

stages.body: Plenty of shader tooling outside this app, including The Book of Shaders and glslCanvas, wires up the same two ideas under different names: u_resolution instead of iResolution, declared as a plain vec2 rather than a vec3, and u_time instead of iTime. Their version of stage one's normalising line reads vec2 uv = gl_FragCoord.xy / u_resolution.xy — no .xy swap needed on the right-hand side, because u_resolution is already two components, unlike our vec3. The maths taught across this module carries over untouched; only the uniform names and the vec2-versus-vec3 declaration change. Recognising u_resolution and u_time as the same concepts as iResolution.xy and iTime is what lets you read a tutorial written for a different sandbox without relearning anything.
stages.source:
vec2 uv = fragCoord / iResolution.xy;
fragColor = vec4(uv.x, uv.y, 0.4, 1.0);
stages.title: The same shader, u_ names

stages.body: GLSL ES 3.00 changes the wrapper this lesson has been describing, not the maths this module taught. A 3.00 program opens with a #version 300 es directive, which this sandbox's wrapper never writes because it targets 1.00 implicitly. Fragment output stops being the built-in gl_FragColor and becomes a variable you declare yourself, typically out vec4 fragColor; at the top level — the same name Shadertoy's mainImage convention already uses for its out parameter, which is not a coincidence. Sampler reads switch from texture2D to a single overloaded texture call. This sandbox stays on 1.00 deliberately: docs/data/shader-sandbox.md notes that some older Android devices do not reliably support WebGL2 features, and a learner on one of those phones deserves a working preview over a marginally newer syntax.
stages.source:
vec2 uv = fragCoord / iResolution.xy;
fragColor = vec4(uv.y, uv.x, 0.6, 1.0);
stages.title: What changes under GLSL ES 3.00

lessons.takeaway: Every stage's source has always been just the body of mainImage; the app supplies precision, the uniform declarations, and a main() that calls your body and writes gl_FragColor for you. Reading real shader code elsewhere means recognising that wrapper even when it uses u_ names instead of i, or targets GLSL ES 3.00 with its own out-variable colour and #version line.
lessons.title: Reading shaders from elsewhere
lessons.tryThis: Take the shader from stage one, paste only its body into a fresh WebGL page with your own wrapper, and see what you have to add for it to compile there.

tutorials.title: Paint by position

modules.description: Turn any continuous measurement into a controlled visual signal.

lessons.intro: Every shader so far has painted a measurement straight onto the screen: a coordinate became a gradient, and that was the whole image. Gradients are honest but shapeless. The first tool for turning a smooth measurement into something with structure is step, which makes a single yes-or-no decision at a threshold you choose. It is the bluntest instrument in the module, and understanding exactly where it is too blunt is what motivates everything after it.

stages.body: Before any decision there has to be something to decide about. This is the horizontal gradient from Module 1, painted into all three colour channels so it reads as grey rather than as a colour: black at the left edge where uv.x is zero, white at the right edge where it reaches one, and every shade in between. Nothing here is new. It is on screen so that the next stage has something recognisable to cut in half, and so you can see precisely which value the threshold is about to be compared against. Keep the left-to-right direction in mind, because every stage in this lesson works along that same axis.
stages.title: Start with a measurement

stages.body: step(edge, value) returns zero when value is below edge and one when it reaches or passes it. Feeding the same gradient through it collapses every shade into one of two answers, so the left half of the screen is pure black and the right half is pure white, with the change happening at exactly the middle where uv.x crosses 0.5. Notice that the gradient has not been removed; it is still being computed, still varying smoothly across every pixel. All that changed is what the shader does with it. Keeping the measurement and the decision separate like this is what lets one measurement drive several different treatments later.
stages.title: step makes the decision

stages.body: The threshold is just a number, so it can be computed rather than typed. Here it is driven by sin(iTime), which swings between minus one and one; multiplying by 0.35 and adding 0.5 keeps the result inside 0.15 to 0.85 so the boundary always stays on screen instead of sliding off an edge and leaving the display a flat colour. The result is a hard vertical edge sweeping left and right. Watch the edge itself rather than the halves: it never softens, never blurs, and never lands between two pixels. Wherever it happens to fall, one column of pixels is black and the very next is white.
stages.title: Move the threshold

stages.body: A vertical edge hides step's weakness, because a vertical line already agrees with the pixel grid. Averaging uv.x and uv.y produces a value that increases toward the top right, so the threshold now falls along a diagonal running from the bottom right corner to the top left. Look closely at that diagonal and you will see a staircase: each row of pixels switches from black to white one step further along than the row beneath it, because every pixel must be entirely one or entirely the other. The measurement crossing the threshold was smooth. The decision made from it was not, and that is what the next lesson fixes.
stages.title: Where step starts to hurt

lessons.takeaway: step(edge, value) returns zero below the threshold and one at or above it, turning a continuous measurement into two flat regions. Subtracting one step from another isolates a band between two thresholds. The decision is instant, which is exactly the problem: on any boundary that is not perfectly aligned with the pixel grid, that instant decision shows up as a visible staircase.
lessons.title: Hard edges with step
lessons.tryThis: Swap the arguments in stage two to step(uv.x, 0.5). Which side goes white now, and can you say why before you look?

lessons.intro: The staircase at the end of the last lesson is not a rendering bug, it is the honest consequence of asking for an instant decision. A pixel is a finite area, and a boundary that falls halfway across one has to be resolved somehow. smoothstep answers by replacing the single threshold with two, and blending across the gap between them instead of jumping. The width of that gap becomes something you control deliberately, rather than something the pixel grid decides for you.

stages.body: This is the closing stage of the previous lesson unchanged, so the comparison over the next few stages is exact rather than remembered. The diagonal boundary runs from the bottom right to the top left, black below it and white above, and each row of pixels flips one position further along than the row below. Put your eye close to the screen if you can. The staircase is small, but on a moving edge it does something worse than look rough: it crawls, because the exact pixel where the flip happens jumps by a whole step at a time rather than sliding.
stages.title: The staircase, one more time

stages.body: Two thresholds either side of the old one, 0.48 and 0.52, give the transition somewhere to happen. Below 0.48 the result is still exactly zero and above 0.52 it is still exactly one, so the flat black and flat white regions are untouched; only the boundary between them changed. The staircase is gone, replaced by a narrow band of greys a few pixels wide. That band is doing the work the pixel grid could not: where a boundary falls partway across a pixel, the pixel can now take a value partway between the two sides instead of being forced to pick one.
stages.title: smoothstep replaces the cliff

stages.body: Moving the two thresholds far apart, to 0.3 and 0.7, shows what they actually control. The midpoint is unchanged, still at 0.5, so the boundary has not moved. What changed is how much of the image is spent crossing it: the flat black region now ends at 0.3, the flat white does not begin until 0.7, and the entire middle 40 percent of the screen is transition. At this width it no longer reads as a soft edge at all, it reads as a gradient with flat regions on either side. Edge and gradient are the same operation with different numbers.
stages.title: The thresholds are the width

stages.body: Keeping the midpoint at 0.5 and animating only the half width makes the edge breathe between crisp and diffuse while staying exactly where it is. The half width runs from 0.02 to 0.30, because sin(iTime) is remapped from its natural minus one to one range into zero to one before being scaled. The important detail is what that width means: it is a distance in the value being tested, not a distance in pixels. The same 0.02 would cover a different number of pixels on a different screen, or if the diagonal were computed at a different scale, which is a limitation Module 3 comes back to with a proper fix.
stages.title: Width lives in the value's units

lessons.takeaway: smoothstep(lower, upper, value) is zero below the lower threshold, one above the upper, and follows a smooth curve between them rather than a straight line. The distance between the two thresholds is the edge width, measured in the same units as the value being tested, not in pixels. A narrow gap reads as a crisp edge without a staircase; a wide gap stops reading as an edge at all and becomes a gradient.
lessons.title: Soft edges with smoothstep
lessons.tryThis: Set both thresholds to the same number in stage two. What does smoothstep turn into, and which earlier stage does the result match?

lessons.intro: So far every result has been a single number painted into all three channels, which is why everything has been grey. mix takes two colours and a factor between them, and returns a colour somewhere along the line joining the two. The colours are usually the easy part of that decision. The factor is where the design actually happens, and the previous two lessons were really about building factors worth feeding in.

stages.body: With a factor of exactly 0.5 the whole screen is one flat colour: the halfway point between a cool cyan and a warm coral, which works out as a muted grey-lavender. It is worth sitting with how unremarkable that is. Both input colours are vivid, the result is not, and nothing has gone wrong. Averaging two saturated colours that sit on opposite sides of the colour space lands you near the middle, and the middle is grey. This is the first hint of what stage four makes unavoidable, and the reason a mix is usually only as good as the factor driving it.
stages.title: Two colours, one constant

stages.body: Replacing the constant with uv.x makes the factor different for every pixel, and the flat colour becomes a blend running the full width of the screen: cool cyan at the left edge where the factor is zero, warm coral at the right where it reaches one, and that same muted grey-lavender from the previous stage passing through the exact middle. Nothing about mix changed. The only difference is that the factor is now a measurement rather than a number, which is the same separation between measuring and deciding that step and smoothstep relied on.
stages.title: A factor that varies across space

stages.body: The colours here are identical to the previous stage. The only change is that the factor now runs through smoothstep between 0.35 and 0.65, and the image is transformed: the left third is flat cool, the right third is flat warm, and all of the colour change is compressed into the middle third. Two vivid regions with a deliberate transition, rather than an even wash where every pixel is a slightly different compromise. This is the whole idea of the module in one stage. The endpoints were never the problem; shaping what travels between them is where the control is.
stages.title: Shape the factor, not the colours

stages.body: Pure red on the left, pure green on the right, and in the middle something most people do not predict. Mixing red and green light gives yellow, so the centre ought to be yellow, and in a sense it is: the halfway value is 0.5 red and 0.5 green. But that is a dark, muddy olive rather than a bright yellow, because mix moves each channel along a straight line and half of full red plus half of full green is only half as much light as full yellow would be. The interpolation is doing exactly what it promises. It just promises less than intuition assumes.
stages.title: One channel at a time

lessons.takeaway: mix(a, b, t) returns a when t is zero, b when t is one, and interpolates each colour channel independently in between. Because the channels are handled separately, the midpoint between two colours is their numerical average, which is often duller or muddier than either endpoint rather than the colour you might expect. Choosing the factor matters more than choosing the endpoints.
lessons.title: Blending with mix
lessons.tryThis: Replace uv.x in stage two with the smoothstep expression from the previous lesson. Where does the blend become flat, and where does all the colour change end up happening?

lessons.intro: Every value so far has happened to stay between zero and one, which is convenient and not guaranteed. Multiply a measurement, subtract an offset, or remap a range, and it will leave those bounds without complaint. The screen quietly forgives that by clipping anything it is handed, which is why the problem stays invisible until the out-of-range value is used for something other than a colour. clamp makes the bound explicit, and the interesting part is which of the two stages below actually needs it.

stages.body: Multiplying the horizontal gradient by 2.5 sends it from zero at the left edge to 2.5 at the right, well past the one that a colour channel can represent. What renders is a gradient that reaches full white about two fifths of the way across, then simply stays white for the remaining three fifths. The information did not survive: every value from one upward, and there are a lot of them, is displayed identically. The screen clipped them for you. That is convenient here and dangerous later, because nothing warned you it happened.
stages.title: A value that leaves the range

stages.body: This renders exactly the same image as the previous stage, and that is the point rather than an oversight. Wrapping the value in clamp between zero and one produces pixel-for-pixel what the framebuffer was already producing on its own. The difference is entirely in where the decision lives: previously the range was enforced by the display, invisibly and at the very last moment, and now it is enforced by code you wrote, at a point you chose. Nothing visible changed because nothing about a colour needed to change. The next stage is where the distinction stops being philosophical.
stages.title: clamp makes the bound explicit

stages.body: Here the same kind of stretched value is used as a factor rather than as a colour, running from minus 0.6 at the left edge to 1.9 at the right. mix does not clip out-of-range factors, it keeps going along the line through both colours and out the other side. To the left the result overshoots past cool into an oversaturated cyan the palette never contained; to the right it overshoots past coral into a hard red. Both extremes are then clipped by the screen, so the edges of the image are flat, blown-out slabs rather than the two colours that were chosen.
stages.title: An unbounded factor breaks a mix

stages.body: One clamp around the factor restores the palette completely. The left quarter of the screen is now exactly the cool cyan that was chosen, the right third is exactly the coral, and the blend between them happens across the middle without ever leaving the two endpoint colours. Compare it against the previous stage: the transition is in the same place and has the same slope, because the arithmetic that produces the factor is unchanged. All that was added is a bound. Clamping the factor is what keeps a design intact; clamping the colour afterwards only cleans up damage that has already happened.
stages.title: Clamp the factor, not the colour

lessons.takeaway: clamp(value, low, high) forces a value into a range instead of leaving it to whatever happens downstream. Writing it changes nothing about how a colour displays, because the framebuffer already clips. It matters when the out-of-range value is used as a factor, because mix does not clip: it extrapolates past both endpoint colours and destroys the palette you chose.
lessons.title: Keeping values in range
lessons.tryThis: In the final stage, clamp to 0.2 and 0.8 instead of 0.0 and 1.0. Which parts of the image stop being pure cool and pure coral, and why?

lessons.intro: Every tool in this module takes a value in some range and expects it in another. smoothstep wants its input near its two thresholds, mix wants a factor between zero and one, and a colour channel wants the same. Remapping is the arithmetic that moves a measurement from the range it naturally occupies into the range the next step needs, and easing is what you do once it is there: bending the journey so it does not have to travel at a constant rate.

stages.body: Multiplying by 0.4 and adding 0.3 takes the usual zero-to-one gradient and lands it in 0.3 to 0.7 instead. The screen shows the consequence directly: the left edge is a mid-dark grey rather than black, the right edge is a light grey rather than white, and the whole image has visibly less contrast than the gradient it came from. Multiplying sets how much of the range gets used and adding sets where that span begins. Those two numbers are the whole of a linear remap, and every remap in this lesson is a rearrangement of them.
stages.title: Squeeze a range

stages.body: Written the other way round, the operation says what it means: subtract where the input starts, divide by how far it spans, and whatever range went in comes out as zero to one. Here the input window is 0.25 to 0.75, so the middle half of the screen carries the full black-to-white ramp. Outside that window the value goes negative on the left and past one on the right, and the screen clips both, which is why the outer quarters are flat black and flat white. That clipping is the previous lesson's problem appearing again, in a form where it happens to be exactly what was wanted.
stages.title: A remap you can read

stages.body: Raising a value between zero and one to a power bends how it travels without changing where it starts or ends, because zero and one are fixed points of any exponent. With an exponent of three the gradient stays noticeably dark far longer than it did: at the middle of the screen the brightness is only 0.125 rather than 0.5, and almost all of the visible change is crowded into the right-hand third. Nothing was clipped and no range was altered. The value passes through the same two endpoints, it just spends its time differently along the way.
stages.title: Bend the ramp

stages.body: The final stage uses everything in the module at once. step splits the screen into two halves by height, and mix chooses which curve each half displays: the lower half carries the power curve from the previous stage, rising from black to white toward the right, while the upper half carries an exponential decay, starting at full white on the left and falling away toward the right. The two are near mirror images, and they meet at a shared dark region a little past the middle, where both happen to sit near 0.13. One measurement, two shapings, and the choice between them made by a third.
stages.title: Two curves, side by side

lessons.takeaway: Subtracting the input's low end and dividing by its span remaps any range onto zero to one, which is the form the rest of the module expects. Once a value is in that range, raising it to a power bends the ramp without leaving the range, since zero and one are unchanged by any exponent. An exponent above one starts slow, below one starts fast, and exp gives a different curve family entirely.
lessons.title: Remapping and easing
lessons.tryThis: Change the exponent in stage three from 3.0 to 1.0. What happens to the image, and what does that tell you about what an exponent of one means?

modules.description: Describe a shape as a reusable field and give it any edge treatment.

lessons.intro: Every shape in this module comes from one idea: instead of asking whether a pixel is inside something, measure how far it is from the edge. That measurement is a distance field — one number per pixel, defined everywhere on the screen rather than only on the shape itself. Module 1 used length to measure the distance from the centre and stopped there. This lesson turns that measurement into something you can build with, and shows why keeping it continuous is exactly what makes it reusable.

stages.body: This paints the distance from the centre straight into all three colour channels, so brightness is distance. The centre reads zero and comes out black, and every direction brightens away from it. Pure white is reached exactly one unit out — and because the aspect line squeezes x, one unit is nearer on the vertical axis than the horizontal. On a tall screen that means the regions above and below the middle clip to flat white, while the left and right edges only reach around 0.56, a mid grey. The rings of equal brightness are perfect circles: that is what a field looks like when you look at it directly.
stages.title: Paint the measurement itself

stages.body: Subtracting 0.5 slides the whole field down by half a unit, so zero no longer sits at the centre — it now falls on a circle of radius 0.5. Inside that circle the value is negative. This is the single most useful move in the module, and the render undersells it badly: negative and zero both display as black, so you see a solid black disc with no visible boundary, fading up to roughly 0.65 grey at the corners and never reaching white at all. The sign is real and the code can read it. The screen simply has no way to show it.
stages.title: Subtract a radius to place the edge

stages.body: step and mix, both from Module 2, turn the invisible sign into two colours. step(0.0, d) returns 0 wherever d is negative and 1 wherever it is not, and mix reads that as a choice between the two colours rather than a blend. The result is a cyan disc of radius 0.5 sitting in a coral field, with a hard edge between them. Nothing about the field changed here — it is the same d as the stage above. Only the way it is read changed, which is the whole reason a field is worth keeping around.
stages.title: Make the sign visible

stages.body: Here the same d again, read a third way. One smoothstep rises just before the edge and another rises just after it, and subtracting the second from the first leaves a band that is 1 only between roughly -0.03 and 0.03. Everything outside that window cancels to 0. What you get is a thin yellow-green ring hanging at radius 0.5 on a near-black background — no fill anywhere, because the band never includes the middle of the disc. A mask could not have produced this. Only a field that still knows how far away it is at every pixel can.
stages.title: One field, a third reading

lessons.takeaway: A distance field is a measurement, not a mask. length(p) gives the distance from the centre, and subtracting a radius moves the zero line out to wherever you want the edge to fall, which is what makes the sign meaningful — negative inside, positive outside. The screen cannot show a negative value, but your code can read it, and every shape in this module is built by choosing where that zero line sits.
lessons.title: Distance as a field
lessons.tryThis: In the last stage, change both smoothstep pairs to widen the ring, then make the ring sit at a different radius without touching the subtraction. Which number controls which?

lessons.intro: The previous lesson produced a circle almost by accident — it fell out of measuring distance from the centre. This lesson takes hold of it properly, so that where the circle sits and how large it is become numbers you set rather than consequences of the coordinate system. Both turn out to be one-line changes, and neither touches the shape of the expression. By the end the circle moves, breathes, and lights the space around it, all from the same single measurement.

stages.body: The subtracted value from the last lesson is now a named variable, which changes nothing about the render and everything about how the code reads. smoothstep turns the field into a fill: it is 1 wherever d is at or below zero, and falls to 0 across the next 0.012, so the disc is cyan with a soft edge a few pixels wide and the background stays near-black. Note the direction — the fill is 1 minus the smoothstep, because d is small inside the shape and large outside, so the raw smoothstep would give you the background instead.
stages.title: Name the radius

stages.body: Subtracting a centre from p before measuring shifts the disc to that centre: it now sits at x 0.2 and y -0.2, which is right of the middle and below it, since p.y runs negative at the bottom of the screen. This is worth pausing on, because Module 1 warned that coordinate transforms often feel backwards. Here it does not — subtract a positive x and the shape moves right. The reason is that you are moving the point of measurement, not the space: you are asking each pixel how far it is from a centre that has itself moved.
stages.title: Move it by moving the coordinate

stages.body: Centre and radius are just floats, so iTime can drive them. sin and cos of the same rate trace a closed ellipse — wider vertically than horizontally here, because the two multipliers differ — and the disc goes round it once every six and a bit seconds. The radius runs on a separate sine at twice that rate, swinging between 0.16 and 0.28, so the disc pulses exactly twice per lap. Nothing structural changed from the stage above. Two constants became expressions, and that is the entire difference between a still image and an animation.
stages.title: Drive both from time

stages.body: A mask would be finished at the edge. A field is not, and this stage spends what is left. The same d feeds a second smoothstep with a far wider range, giving a value that is 1 at the edge and does not reach 0 until half a unit out, which paints a teal halo fading to background by radius 0.76. The bright fill is then mixed over the top so the disc itself stays clean. Halfway through the halo the two colours sit at even weight. This costs one extra line precisely because the measurement never stopped being available.
stages.title: The field outside the shape

lessons.takeaway: A circle needs two numbers you control: a centre, subtracted from the coordinate before measuring, and a radius, subtracted from the measurement afterwards. Order matters — the first moves the shape, the second resizes it. Because both are ordinary floats, anything that can produce a float can drive them, including iTime. And the field keeps meaning something outside the shape, which is where effects like a glow come from for free.
lessons.title: A circle you control

lessons.intro: A circle is the easy case, because distance from a point is exactly what length already computes. A rectangle has corners and flat sides, and no single built-in measures it. Building one introduces two functions that do far more work in this module than their names suggest: abs, which folds the plane so you only have to think about one quadrant, and max, which is how you say that two conditions must both hold. The rounding trick at the end costs one subtraction.

stages.body: abs applied to a vec2 takes the absolute value of each component separately, which mirrors the left half onto the right and the bottom half onto the top. Painting the folded coordinate shows it plainly: the centre is dark blue where both components are zero, red grows toward the left and right edges, green grows toward the top and bottom, and all four corners land on the same pale yellow-green. Top-left, top-right, bottom-left and bottom-right are pixel-identical. Anything you build from the folded coordinate is symmetric about both axes without you arranging for it.
stages.title: abs folds the plane

stages.body: Subtracting a half-size from the folded coordinate gives a value per axis that is negative inside the box's extent on that axis. max of the two is negative only when both are, which is precisely the rectangle: 0.68 wide and 0.44 tall, in yellow-green on near-black. That is max used as a logical and. The inside of this field is correct, but the outside is not quite a distance — diagonally past a corner it reports the larger of the two gaps rather than the true one, which the next stage both shows and fixes.
stages.title: max means both at once

stages.body: max here takes a vector and a float, clamping each component up to zero, so inside the box both components are zeroed and length returns exactly 0. Outside, the surviving components form the offset to the nearest point on the box, and length measures it truly. The wide smoothstep exposes the difference: the halo's contours curve around the corners in quarter circles. Under the previous stage's max they would have run square. The fill is identical either way, which is why this error hides until the moment you use the field for anything beyond filling.
stages.title: Measure the outside properly

stages.body: Subtracting a constant from a distance field moves its zero line outward by that amount in every direction at once, and around a corner every direction means a quarter circle. So rounding is free: shrink the half-size by the rounding first, then subtract the rounding from the field. The shrink is what keeps the outer size unchanged — this box still measures 0.68 by 0.44, exactly like the last two stages, but now with corners of radius 0.1. Push rounding up to the smaller half-size and the box becomes a capsule, then a circle.
stages.title: Rounding is a subtraction

lessons.takeaway: abs mirrors the plane into all four quadrants, so a box only has to be described once and comes out symmetric. max of the two folded axes is negative only where both are, which is the rectangle. Taking length of the outside part measures the corners properly, where the plain max only approximates them. Rounding is then a subtraction: shrink the box by the corner radius, then subtract that radius from the field, and the outer size is preserved.
lessons.title: Boxes and rounded boxes

lessons.intro: Two shapes drawn one over the other are two shapes that happen to overlap. Combined as fields they become a single shape, with one continuous boundary that every later effect can read as a whole. The difference matters more than it first appears, and this lesson makes it visible before naming the three operators that do the work. All three are functions you already have, and all three are one line long.

stages.body: Two discs of radius 0.26, offset left and right of centre, each turned into its own fill and painted in turn. Because the coral disc is mixed last it covers the cyan one where they overlap, leaving a cyan crescent on the left and a whole coral circle on the right. It looks like a composition, and for painting purposes it is one. But there is no value anywhere in this shader that describes the pair as a single shape, so nothing here can be given an outline, a glow, or a rounded join.
stages.title: Drawn separately is not combined

stages.body: min of the two fields keeps whichever surface is nearer, and the result is a union: one yellow-green shape with a single unbroken outline, pinched slightly at the waist where the two circles meet. Only the colouring collapsed to one fill — the geometry did not change at all. This is why the operators are worth learning as field operations rather than as drawing tricks: min produced a new field, so it can be fed to a ring, a glow, or another min, exactly like the fields it was built from.
stages.title: min unites

stages.body: One character changes and the meaning inverts. max is negative only where both fields are negative, so what survives is the overlap alone: a tall pointed oval, roughly 0.2 wide and 0.41 tall, meeting in sharp cusps at the top and bottom where the two circles cross. Everything either disc had to itself is gone. This is the same max that built the box two lessons ago, doing the same job — insisting both conditions hold at once — on whole shapes rather than on two axes.
stages.title: max intersects

stages.body: Negating a field swaps its sign everywhere, so inside becomes outside and the shape turns inside out. Intersecting the left disc with the inverted right one therefore keeps what is inside the left and outside the right: a crescent, thick at the far left, opening to the right, with horns reaching the points where the circles cross. There is no subtract function, and there does not need to be. Reverse the two and you get the mirrored crescent, which is a useful reminder that this operation, unlike the other two, cares about order.
stages.title: Negation subtracts

lessons.takeaway: min unites two fields, max intersects them, and max against a negated field subtracts one from the other. Each returns a field, not a picture, so the result composes exactly like the shapes that went into it and every treatment from earlier lessons still applies. Negating a field swaps its inside and outside, which is why subtraction is intersection with a complement rather than an operator of its own.
lessons.title: Combining shapes

lessons.intro: Every stage so far has softened its edge with the same hand-picked 0.012, and every one of them looked fine, because nothing has changed scale yet. That number is measured in the field's units, not in pixels, so the moment a shape grows or shrinks it stops being right — too soft at one size, jagged at another. This lesson makes that failure visible and then removes the guesswork entirely, using a function that can tell you how large a pixel is.

stages.body: This is the same disc and the same 0.012 as the rest of the module, and there is nothing wrong with it. The edge is a fraction under one percent of the preview's height, which on a surface a few hundred pixels tall works out to a small handful of pixels: soft enough not to stair-step, tight enough to read as a clean edge. The number was chosen by eye and it does its job. Worth noticing before the next stage is that nothing in the code knows how big a pixel is.
stages.title: Fine, at exactly one size

stages.body: Multiplying the coordinate by a changing zoom makes the disc grow and shrink — a larger multiplier packs more field into the same screen, so the disc gets smaller. The edge width is still 0.012 in field units, so on screen it shrinks and grows with everything else, by more than four times across the cycle. Watch the boundary rather than the disc: at its largest the edge is a visible blur, and at its smallest it tightens until it starts to stair-step. One constant cannot be correct at both ends.
stages.title: Change scale and it breaks

stages.body: fwidth reports roughly how much a value changes between one pixel and the next, by comparing against the neighbouring pixels being shaded alongside this one. Given a distance field it therefore answers the question the last stage could not: how far, in field units, is one pixel? Smoothstepping from minus that width to plus it spans about two pixels at every zoom. The disc breathes exactly as before, and the edge now holds the same crispness throughout. The 0.012 is gone, and with it the assumption about scale.
stages.title: fwidth measures a pixel

stages.body: The whole module in nine lines. A rounded box built from abs and max, a circle placed to overlap its top edge, min uniting them into one shape, and fwidth keeping the outline honest while the zoom drives it. The join between the box and the circle is seamless because they were combined as fields rather than drawn in sequence. Nothing here is new — every line is from an earlier lesson — and that is the point: fields compose, and the edge treatment does not care how the field was assembled.
stages.title: Everything at once

lessons.takeaway: A hand-tuned edge width is tied to one scale and one screen. fwidth reports how much a value changes across a single pixel, so smoothstep between minus and plus that width gives an edge about two pixels wide no matter how the shape is scaled or what resolution it is rendered at. It works on any field, however that field was built, which is the last thing that makes distance fields worth the trouble.
lessons.title: Edges that survive scaling

modules.description: Drive colour from any scalar field the shader produces.

lessons.intro: Every stage so far has written a vec3 and moved on. This lesson stops and looks at what those three numbers actually are: independent channels, each running from 0 to 1, each clipped hard at both ends. Then it takes on the part most introductions skip entirely — the value you store is not the amount of light the screen emits, and knowing the difference is what stops colour arithmetic from surprising you later.

stages.body: Red is driven by uv.x, green by uv.y, and blue is pinned at a constant quarter. Nothing couples them, which is the point: the corners land on four completely different colours from one expression. Bottom-left is near-black with a faint blue cast, bottom-right is red, top-left is green, and top-right is where both ramps arrive at once and the result goes pale yellow-white. Every colour on this screen is a coordinate in a cube, and the shader is simply reading off two of its axes from position.
stages.title: Three numbers that ignore each other

stages.body: This ramp deliberately overshoots at both ends. Doubling uv.x and pulling it down by a half puts zero at a quarter of the way across and one at three quarters, so the left quarter of the screen is asked for negative brightness and the right quarter for more than full. Both requests are flattened: a solid black band, a gradient through the middle, then a solid white band. The hardware clamps for you when writing the final colour, which is convenient here and a trap the moment a value like this is used as a mix factor instead.
stages.title: The range is 0 to 1

stages.body: An ordinary black-to-white ramp, and the interesting part is not on screen but in what the middle of it means. At the halfway point the stored value is 0.5, and the display emits about a fifth of its maximum light — not half. Yet it reads as a convincing middle grey. Both facts are true because the encoding is not linear in light: it spends far more of its range on dark values, where vision is most sensitive, and comparatively little on bright ones. The number tracks appearance closely and light only loosely.
stages.source:
vec2 uv = fragCoord / iResolution.xy;

fragColor = vec4(vec3(uv.x), 1.0);
stages.title: The numbers are not light

stages.body: The bottom half is the ramp from the last stage. The top half raises it to the power 2.2, which converts it into a ramp that is even in light rather than even in appearance — and it looks nothing alike. Both agree at the two ends, because zero and one are fixed points, but everywhere between the top band is far darker: at the midpoint it drops from 0.5 to 0.22, and a quarter of the way across from 0.25 to 0.05, crushing the shadows into near-black. Neither band is wrong. They are answering different questions.
stages.title: See the difference

lessons.takeaway: A colour is three independent numbers, each meaningful between 0 and 1 and flattened outside it. What they are not is light: a stored 0.5 emits roughly a fifth of the display's brightness, yet reads as middle grey, because the encoding deliberately spends more of its range on dark values to match how vision works. Arithmetic on these numbers is therefore arithmetic on appearance, not on light, which is usually what you want and occasionally not.
lessons.title: Colour as three numbers
lessons.tryThis: In the second stage, wrap the ramp in clamp before it reaches the colour. The picture will not change at all — which tells you something about what the hardware was already doing for you.

lessons.intro: Module 2 introduced mix with a constant factor and then with uv.x, which produced a gradient. Module 3 spent five lessons building fields — numbers that vary across the screen and mean something everywhere. This lesson connects the two, and the connection is the whole point of the module: any field can be a mix factor, so anything you can measure, you can colour by. Nothing new is introduced. The combination is what is new.

stages.body: The starting point, and the only stage here that uses a coordinate as its factor. A cool blue on the left, a warm orange on the right, and uv.x sliding between them. The midpoint is worth looking at rather than assuming: it is not a vivid colour but a muted mauve-grey around 0.56, 0.46, 0.43, because mixing opposite hues channel by channel pulls all three toward each other. That flattening in the middle is characteristic of straight-line blending and is the reason the next lessons reach for palettes instead.
stages.title: A gradient is a mix across space

stages.body: Here the factor is a circle's distance field rather than a coordinate. The field runs negative inside and positive out, so adding a half shifts it into useful territory and clamp keeps it there. The result is a soft radial gradient: warm pink at the centre where the field sits lowest, passing through the circle's nominal edge at exactly the halfway colour, and settling into dark navy by the time the distance reaches 0.9. There is no hard edge anywhere on this screen, and no shape either — only a measurement being read as colour.
stages.title: Any field will do

stages.body: mix only ever takes two colours, so a third arrives by mixing again over the result. The first smoothstep runs across the left half and takes deep navy to rose; the second runs across the right half and takes that rose to pale gold. Because each smoothstep is flat outside its own window, the two never fight over the same pixels. The midpoint lands exactly on the rose, and the easing at each end of both windows is what keeps the two joins from showing as creases.
stages.title: Three stops from two mixes

stages.body: Two readings of one field, doing different jobs. fwidth and a narrow smoothstep give the crisp fill from Module 3, deciding where the disc is. The same field, negated and divided by the radius, gives a value that runs from 1 at the centre to 0 at the rim, deciding what colour the disc is there — pale gold in the middle falling to deep red at its edge. The background mix then places the whole thing. A shape and its shading from a single measurement, which is what fields are for.
stages.title: Colour inside the shape

lessons.takeaway: A gradient is a mix whose factor varies across space, and the factor does not have to be a coordinate. A distance field, a fill, or any scalar the shader can compute will drive it, provided the value is brought into the 0 to 1 range first. Chaining two mixes gives a third colour without a third function, and colouring a shape by its own field is the same idea turned inward.
lessons.title: Mixing across space

lessons.intro: Reducing a colour to a single brightness number sounds like it should be an average, and almost every first attempt is. It is also wrong in a way that is easy to see once you look for it: the eye is far more sensitive to green than to blue, by roughly a factor of ten. This lesson builds a deliberately colourful test image, measures it the obvious way, measures it the way vision does, and then uses the result to push contrast around a pivot.

stages.body: The test image, built entirely from Module 3. Three circles, each written into a single colour channel, each antialiased with its own fwidth. Because the channels are independent the overlaps do the arithmetic themselves: red and green together make yellow, red and blue make magenta, green and blue make cyan, and the small region where all three meet comes out white. Nothing here is new, and that is deliberate — the next three stages change only how this image is measured, never how it is made.
stages.title: Three lights to measure

stages.body: Averaging the three channels and painting the result as grey. Look at what happened to the three circles: every one of them became the same mid grey, exactly a third, because each is a single channel at full strength and the average cannot tell them apart. The two-way overlaps all land on two thirds and the centre on white. This is a defensible measure of how much colour is present. It is not a measure of how bright anything looks, and holding it beside the previous stage makes that obvious.
stages.title: The obvious answer

stages.body: dot multiplies two vectors component by component and adds the results, which is exactly the shape of a weighted sum, so the whole measurement fits in one call. These particular weights are the Rec. 709 luma coefficients, and the three circles now separate hard: green reads at 0.72, red at 0.21, and blue at 0.07 — barely distinguishable from the background. That spread is not a stylistic choice, it is roughly the sensitivity of human vision, and it is why a blue of the same nominal strength as a green looks so much darker.
stages.title: Weights that match the eye

stages.body: Contrast is not a multiply. Multiplying scales everything toward black, which darkens rather than separates, so the trick is to subtract a pivot first, scale, and add the pivot back. Here the scale sweeps from 0.2 to 3.0. Above one the colours push apart and saturate; below one everything collapses toward the pivot, and watch the background — it is not immune, lifting off black to a flat grey as the scale falls. clamp is doing real work at both extremes, which is precisely the overshoot Module 2 warned about.
stages.title: Contrast around a pivot

lessons.takeaway: Averaging the three channels weights them equally, which vision does not: green carries about 0.72 of perceived brightness, red 0.21, and blue only 0.07. dot with those weights is the standard Rec. 709 luma, and it costs exactly one instruction. Contrast is then a scaling around a pivot rather than a multiply, since multiplying darkens everything, and the result needs clamping because pushing away from the pivot leaves the range at both ends.
lessons.title: Brightness that matches vision

lessons.intro: Mixing between two or three fixed colours works, but the colours have to be chosen and stored, and the midpoints tend to go muddy. A palette function replaces the list with an expression: give it a number, get a colour, with no table and no branching. The one used here is built from three cosines, needs four vec3 parameters, and once assembled it will happily take any scalar the shader can produce — a coordinate, a distance, or time.

stages.body: Before three channels, one. Multiplying uv.x by two pi turns the width of the screen into exactly one full turn of a cosine, and the half-plus-half pattern lifts its natural minus-one-to-one swing into the 0 to 1 a colour needs. The result is white at both edges, black in the middle, and smooth throughout. That smoothness is the reason cosines are used here rather than a ramp: the value and its slope both come back around, so a palette built this way never shows a seam.
stages.title: One cosine, one channel

stages.body: The same wave on all three channels, offset by the phase vector d so they peak at different places. Red peaks at both edges, green a third of the way across, blue two thirds — so the screen reads as a spectrum sweeping from salmon through green to blue and back. Every operation here is on a vec3, so one cos call does all three channels at once. Set d to three equal numbers and the whole thing collapses back to grey, which is a quick way to confirm the phase is doing the work.
stages.title: Three cosines, one palette

stages.body: Driving d from time slides the phase, and the whole spectrum drifts steadily leftward across the screen, wrapping seamlessly because a cosine has no start. The other three are worth predicting before you try them: a moves the middle brightness, so lowering it darkens everything without changing the hues; b sets how far the swing reaches, and at zero the palette flattens to the single colour a; c counts cycles, so raising it to 2.0 fits two full spectra across the same width. Each is independent of the others.
stages.title: What the four parameters do

stages.body: The palette never asked where its number came from, so this hands it a distance instead of a coordinate. With c at 2.0 a little over two full cycles fit between the centre and the far corner, drawing concentric rings of colour, and the drifting phase pulls those rings steadily inward. Swap length for any field from Module 3 — a box, a union, a subtraction — and the rings follow that shape's contours instead. This is the module's goal in five lines: colour driven by any scalar the shader can produce.
stages.title: Feed it any scalar

lessons.takeaway: A cosine palette is a plus b times the cosine of two pi times c times t plus d, evaluated on all three channels at once. a sets the middle brightness, b how far it swings, c how many cycles fit in the range, and d the per-channel phase that turns three identical waves into a spectrum. Because it is a function of one number, anything scalar can drive it, which is the whole module in a line.
lessons.title: Palettes as functions
