modules.description: Transform, tile, and vary coordinate space before a shape is ever evaluated.

lessons.intro: Every module so far has built the same three lines of coordinate setup and then left them alone. This one treats those coordinates as material. Change what a pixel believes its position to be and every shape evaluated afterwards moves, without a single shape knowing about it. The catch is a sign: whatever you do to the coordinate, the picture appears to do the opposite, and this lesson makes that concrete before the next four rely on it.

stages.body: This is Module 3's placement, revisited on purpose. Subtracting an offset from the coordinate before measuring puts the disc at that offset, up and to the right of centre, and it reads exactly as written: the numbers in the vector are where the shape ends up. Nothing feels reversed here, which is worth noticing now, because the next stage performs the same subtraction in a different place and the result moves the opposite way. The arithmetic will not change. The framing will.
stages.title: Naming where a shape sits

stages.body: The same offset, the same disc, and the shape lands in the opposite corner — down and to the left. The difference is that the offset is now added to the coordinate itself and the disc is measured from zero, so nothing was placed anywhere. Every pixel was simply told it is a quarter further right and a little higher than it really is, and a pixel that believes it is at the origin is the one that draws the centre of the disc. Add to the coordinate, and the picture moves away.
stages.title: Moving the space instead

stages.body: Two discs are placed at fixed positions in a space that is itself sliding left and right. Neither disc knows this — both are written exactly as in the first stage — yet the pair travels together, and always against the shift: when the shift runs positive the discs move left. That is the payoff for transforming coordinates rather than positions. One line moved a whole scene, and a scene of fifty shapes would have cost the same line.
stages.title: One change, every shape

stages.body: Here the two ideas sit in the same shader. The camera vector moves the space and the placement vector names a spot inside it, so the disc orbits the position it was given rather than resting on it. Reading it as two steps keeps the sign straight: first decide where the observer is, then place the shape relative to that. The disc traces a small ellipse, opposite in direction to the camera, and never leaves the screen because the two vectors were sized to fit together.
stages.title: Both at once

lessons.takeaway: Transforming the coordinate transforms every shape downstream of it at once, because you are relabelling where each pixel thinks it is rather than moving anything. Subtracting a vector before measuring names where a shape should sit and reads naturally; adding one to the whole space slides the entire scene the other way. Both are the same arithmetic seen from different ends, and the inverse feel comes from which one you think you are doing.
lessons.title: Moving the coordinate system
lessons.tryThis: In the third stage, change the plus to a minus and nothing else. The two discs will still slide together — but the direction they travel relative to the shift will have swapped.

lessons.intro: Translation was addition. Scale is a multiply, and rotation needs a two-by-two matrix — the first time this course has used one. Both obey the inverse rule from the previous lesson, and both share a second property that catches people out far more often: they happen about the coordinate origin, wherever that happens to be. That is the real reason the centring line has been sitting at the top of every stage since Module 1.

stages.body: Multiplying the coordinate by 1.6 shrinks the rounded box to five eighths of its written size, because a pixel now reports a position further from the origin than it truly is and therefore falls outside a shape it would otherwise have been inside. Same inverse rule as translation, same reason. This is also exactly what the zoom in Module 3's last lesson was doing, named properly at last: a scale applied to space rather than to any particular shape.
stages.title: Scale is a multiply

stages.body: A rotation matrix is four numbers built from one angle, and GLSL fills a matrix column by column rather than row by row — so this argument order reads as cos, sin down the first column and minus sin, cos down the second. That combination turns the coordinate counter-clockwise, which by the inverse rule turns the box you see clockwise, here by about thirty-four degrees. Get the two middle arguments the wrong way round and everything still compiles and still rotates; it simply goes the other way.
stages.title: Rotation is a matrix

stages.body: Subtracting a pivot before rotating moves the origin, and the small disc now swings in a circle around a point below and right of centre instead of spinning where it stands. Nothing about the rotation changed — only where zero was when it happened. This is why centring comes first everywhere else in the course: with the usual centred coordinate, zero is the middle of the screen, so shapes turn in place. Skip that line and rotate raw uv, and everything orbits the bottom-left corner.
stages.title: Rotation happens about zero

stages.body: Three transforms in a row, each written as a reassignment so the order is plain: place, spin, breathe. The box slides side to side, turns steadily clockwise, and pulses between roughly six tenths and nine tenths of its written size. Read the chain downward and you are describing what happens to the coordinate; read it upward and you are describing what happens to the shape. Both readings are useful, and mixing them halfway through is the reliable way to get lost.
stages.title: Chaining transforms

lessons.takeaway: Multiplying the coordinate by a number scales every shape by its reciprocal, and multiplying by mat2 of cos, sin, minus sin, cos turns the picture clockwise. GLSL builds matrices column by column, so that argument order is the one that gives a counter-clockwise turn of the coordinate and therefore a clockwise turn of what you see. Both operate about zero, so where zero sits decides whether a shape spins in place or orbits.
lessons.title: Rotation and scale

lessons.intro: A point can be described by how far across and how far up it is, or by how far out and at what angle. The second description has been half-present since Module 3, because length is already the distance half of it. This lesson adds the other half with atan, which hands back an angle, and then uses that angle to drive pattern — spokes, petals and spirals that would be awkward to express any other way.

stages.body: Radius goes into red and angle into green, scaled from its natural minus pi to pi range into 0 to 1. Red therefore grows in circles outward from the centre, clipping to full before the corners. Green sweeps once around, and it is the seam that matters: along the negative x axis, running left from the centre, green jumps from full to nothing in one pixel. That discontinuity is not a bug in atan. It is what happens when a quantity that wraps is read as one that does not.
stages.title: Radius and angle, painted

stages.body: Multiplying the angle by eight and taking a cosine gives eight bright spokes radiating from the centre, evenly spaced, extending to every edge. The seam from the last stage has gone, and not by accident: a cosine takes the same value at both ends of the angle's range, so the value never jumps. Because eight is a whole number the slopes match there too, so nothing creases either. Try 8.5 and a crease appears along the negative x axis, faint but unmistakable once seen.
stages.title: Angle drives pattern

stages.body: A circle is every point whose radius equals a constant. Let that constant vary with angle instead and the circle becomes a flower: five rounded petals, reaching 0.38 at their tips and pulling in to 0.18 between them. The subtraction is the same shape as every distance field so far, which is why fwidth still antialiases it correctly. It is no longer a true distance — the value grows more slowly than real distance along the petal flanks — but for filling a shape that difference never surfaces.
stages.title: A radius that depends on angle

stages.body: Adding radius into the same cosine that reads angle tilts the spokes into arms, because a point one step further out needs slightly more angle to stay on the same crest. Three arms, coiling outward, turning steadily as time shifts the phase. The colour comes from Module 4's palette fed by the same value, so the arms sweep through a spectrum rather than fading to grey. Set the radius multiplier to zero and the spiral unwinds back into the plain spokes of two stages ago.
stages.title: Both at once makes a spiral

lessons.takeaway: atan of y and x gives the angle from the positive x axis, running from minus pi to pi, and length gives the radius. Together they are a complete description of a point. The angle wraps, so reading it directly leaves a hard seam along the negative x axis; feeding it through a cosine hides that, and an integer number of cycles removes even the crease, because only then do the slopes match where the two ends meet.
lessons.title: Polar coordinates

lessons.intro: One shape can be made to appear hundreds of times without being written hundreds of times, and without a loop. The trick is to fold the coordinate: keep only the fractional part of a scaled position, and every whole-number square of the plane collapses onto the same small patch. Draw one shape in that patch and it appears in all of them. The fold is a single function call, and the interesting part is what it does at the joins.

stages.body: Scaling uv.x by four and keeping only the fractional part turns one ramp into four. Each runs black to almost-white and then drops back to black instantly, because 0.999 keeps its 0.999 while 1.0 becomes 0.0 exactly. Those four hard resets are the cell boundaries, and everything in this lesson happens between them. Note that no shape and no branch was involved: the repetition is a property of the coordinate now, not of anything drawn on it.
stages.title: fract keeps what is after the point

stages.body: The same fold on both axes at once cuts the plane into squares a third of a unit across, and subtracting a half moves each square's origin to its middle. One circle written once therefore appears in every cell — a grid roughly three and a third wide by six tall on a portrait screen. The cells are square rather than stretched because the aspect line at the top made the units equal in both directions, which is the same reason circles have been round since Module 1.
stages.title: Fold both axes into cells

stages.body: Here the half is not subtracted, so each cell's origin sits at its bottom-left corner, and the circle is placed near the right-hand edge with a radius large enough to overhang it. Every circle is sliced flat down its right side, and the piece that was cut off does not reappear in the neighbour. That is the one real constraint of this technique: a cell has no knowledge of the cells beside it, so a shape either fits inside one or gets cut.
stages.title: What happens at the join

stages.body: Centred cells again, with the radius driven by time so the grid pulses between 0.06 and 0.3. Watch what the whole grid does rather than any one circle: every cell pulses in perfect unison, because every cell is running the same expression on the same local coordinate and has no way to tell itself apart from its neighbours. That is not a limitation of tiling so much as a missing ingredient, and supplying it is the whole of the next lesson.
stages.title: Every cell, identically

lessons.takeaway: fract keeps the part after the decimal point, so fract of a scaled coordinate wraps back to zero at every whole number and cuts the plane into identical cells. Multiplying before the fold sets how many cells there are; subtracting a half after it puts the origin in the middle of each cell, which is where shapes want to be. Anything reaching past a cell boundary is cut off rather than continued, because the neighbouring cell is a separate copy that knows nothing about it.
lessons.title: Tiling with fract

lessons.intro: The previous lesson threw something away. Splitting a coordinate into cells produces two halves — where you are within a cell, and which cell that is — and only the first was kept. Recovering the second takes one more function, and it turns a grid of identical copies into a grid whose every member can differ. This lesson also marks the honest edge of what position alone can do, which is exactly where the next module begins.

stages.body: floor rounds down to the whole number below, so across an entire cell it returns one unchanging pair. Painting that pair straight into red and green gives flat blocks of colour rather than gradients — proof that the value really is constant within each cell and steps only at the boundaries. The identities run negative on the left and bottom, so the scale and offset are chosen to land all six rows evenly between 0 and 1, which is why no two rows share a shade.
stages.title: floor names the cell

stages.body: Scale once, then take floor and fract of the same value: identity and local position, no information lost. The local half draws the circle exactly as before; the identity half feeds Module 4's palette, so each cell is tinted by its own coordinates. Cells sharing a diagonal share an identity sum and therefore a colour, which is why the tint sweeps in bands running from lower-right to upper-left rather than varying cell by cell in every direction.
stages.title: Keep both halves

stages.body: The same identity now offsets each cell's place in a time cycle instead of its colour. Every circle still pulses at the same rate, but each starts at a different point in that cycle, so a wave appears to travel diagonally across the grid. Nothing here is animated per cell — there is one sine, evaluated once — and the illusion of a travelling wave comes entirely from feeding position into its phase, which is the same idea the spiral used two lessons ago.
stages.title: Identity can drive anything

stages.body: The circle is placed off-centre so it has a handedness, and alternate cells flip it: mod of the identity sum gives a checkerboard of zeros and ones, and negating the local x mirrors those cells. The result reads as a woven pattern rather than a repeated stamp. It is also as far as position alone goes — every cell here is still a fixed function of where it is, so the pattern stays perfectly regular. Breaking that regularity is what randomness is for.
stages.title: Mirroring, and the edge of position

lessons.takeaway: floor of a scaled coordinate gives the cell's integer identity, and fract gives the position inside it; together they lose nothing. Because the identity is constant across a whole cell, anything derived from it is constant there too, so it can drive colour, size or phase per cell. All such variation is still a function of position, so it stays regular by construction — irregularity needs a source of randomness, which is Module 6.
lessons.title: Cell identity

lessons.intro: Module 5 ended by naming its own ceiling: everything a cell could know about itself was a tidy function of where it sat, so every pattern came out regular. This lesson supplies the missing ingredient. A shader has no random number generator and no memory between frames, so what it uses instead is a function that scrambles its input so thoroughly the output looks random — while still returning the same answer every single time it is asked.

stages.body: This is the first stage in the course to declare a function, which it can do because helpers sit above mainImage where GLSL allows definitions. hash takes a cell coordinate and returns a value between 0 and 1. Feeding it floored positions gives one value per cell, and the screen fills with roughly two thousand square specks of unrelated brightness — television static. There is no seed and no state anywhere in this shader. Every speck is simply a function of where it is.
stages.title: A number from a position

stages.body: Scrolling the coordinate before flooring it slides the static sideways, a whole cell at a time. Watch one bright speck: it keeps its exact brightness as it travels, because that brightness belongs to a cell identity that is moving, not to a pixel being re-rolled each frame. If this were a real random generator the screen would boil instead, a fresh field every frame. Determinism is not a limitation being worked around here. It is the property that makes the value reusable.
stages.title: Attached to the coordinate, not the frame

stages.body: The same expression with the multiplier and fract removed, on a continuous coordinate. What comes back is not random at all: about twenty-five fine stripes, running almost horizontally and tilted around nine degrees, because the dot product collapses the plane onto one axis and the sine repeats along it. The randomness is not in the sine. It arrives when that smooth output is multiplied by a large number and only the fractional part kept, which throws neighbouring inputs to unrelated places.
stages.title: What is inside the trick

stages.body: The tiling from the previous module, with the cell identity now passed through hash before it decides anything. Each circle takes a radius between 0.1 and 0.42, and the grid reads as genuinely irregular rather than as a pattern — no diagonal banding, no repeat, nothing the eye can predict from one cell to the next. The only change from Module 5's last lesson is one function call. Identity gave each cell a name; the hash turns that name into something unrepeatable.
stages.title: The thing Module 5 could not do

lessons.takeaway: A hash turns a coordinate into a value that looks random but is not: the same input always gives the same output, which is exactly what a shader needs when nothing is remembered between frames. The usual construction takes a dot product to collapse two numbers into one, a sine to fold it into a bounded range, and a large multiplier before fract to make neighbouring inputs land far apart.
lessons.title: Deterministic randomness
lessons.tryThis: Change 43758.5453 to something small, like 7.0, in the first stage. The static collapses into visible structure, which shows how much of the apparent randomness is doing violence to the sine rather than coming from it.

lessons.intro: A hash gives one unrelated number per cell, which is why the last lesson looked like static: neighbouring cells know nothing about each other. Noise is what you get when those isolated values are made to agree along the way between them. The recipe is short — a random value at every lattice point, then interpolation across each cell — and the quality of the result turns almost entirely on which interpolation you choose.

stages.body: The starting point, at a much coarser scale than the static two stages ago so individual cells are large enough to study. Flooring throws away where inside the cell a pixel is, so every pixel in a cell gets the identical value and the result is a mosaic of flat squares about four and a half across by eight down. Everything from here is about recovering that discarded fraction and using it to travel smoothly between neighbouring squares.
stages.title: One value per cell

stages.body: Both halves of the split from Module 5 are back, and this time the fraction does the work. Three mixes blend the four corner values: two across the bottom and top edges, then one between those. The flat squares are gone, but something has replaced them — a faint diamond quilting, with visible creases running along every cell boundary. The value is continuous there; its rate of change is not, and the eye is far better at spotting a kink than a step.
stages.title: Blend between the four corners

stages.body: One line is different: the fraction is bent through f times f times three minus two f before being used as a blend factor. That expression is smoothstep, written out — the very curve Module 2 introduced — and its useful property here is that its slope is zero at both 0 and 1. Arriving at a cell boundary with no rate of change means the neighbouring cell can pick up without a kink, and the quilting vanishes into soft, rolling blobs.
stages.title: Smooth the fraction, not the value

stages.body: Subtracting a half turns the noise into something with a sign, which is the shape of every field from Module 3 — negative in some places, positive in others, zero along a boundary. fwidth antialiases that boundary exactly as it did for a circle, and the result reads as coastline: irregular islands with soft edges, drifting as time slides the coordinate. Noise became geometry without a single new idea, because a field never cared where its numbers came from.
stages.title: Noise as a shape

lessons.takeaway: Value noise puts a hashed value at every whole-numbered point and blends between the four surrounding it. Straight linear blending leaves the slope jumping at every cell edge, which the eye reads as a grid of creases; running the fraction through the same smoothstep curve from Module 2 flattens the slope to zero at the boundaries and the creases disappear. The result is continuous, repeatable, and cheap.
lessons.title: Value noise

lessons.intro: Value noise works, and at a glance it looks fine. Look at it for a while, though, and a grid starts to show through: light and dark patches keep landing on the same square lattice, because that is precisely where the hashed values live. Gradient noise fixes this by storing something different at each lattice point — not a value, but a direction — and reading the result off the slope instead. The change costs one dot product per corner.

stages.body: hash2 returns two numbers rather than one, a random vector somewhere in the square from minus one to one. Each corner contributes the dot product of its vector with the offset from that corner to the pixel, which is zero when the pixel sits on the corner and grows as it moves away. Interpolating those four contributions gives a field that hovers around a mid grey, rarely reaching pure black or white, and whose soft patches sit at no particular angle.
stages.title: Slopes instead of heights

stages.body: Value noise on the bottom half, gradient noise on the top, at the same scale and with a hairline between them. The bottom is higher in contrast, reaching much closer to black and white, and its light patches line up into rows and columns once you look for them. The top is gentler and its patches drift at arbitrary angles. Neither is better in the abstract, but only one of them stops looking like a grid the longer you stare.
stages.title: The two, side by side

stages.body: This marks in red everywhere the noise sits within a whisker of 0.5. What appears is a web of curves rather than isolated dots, because 0.5 is a contour that runs continuously across the field — but look where those curves cross. Every intersection lands exactly on a lattice point, because there the offset from the nearest corner is zero, so all four dot products vanish and the value is pinned to 0.5. Value noise puts its extremes on the lattice; gradient noise puts its midpoint there.
stages.title: Zero at every lattice point

stages.body: The noise drives Module 4's palette instead of a grey, and drifts slowly as time moves the coordinate. Because gradient noise keeps to the middle of its range the palette never sweeps its full spectrum, so the image stays within a related band of colour rather than cycling through everything — which is usually what you want and is worth knowing before you go looking for a bug that is not there. Widen the range by scaling around 0.5.
stages.title: Put it to work

lessons.takeaway: Gradient noise hashes a random vector at each lattice point and takes its dot product with the offset from that point, so the result is always exactly zero at the lattice itself and gets all its variation from between the points. That is the opposite of value noise, whose extremes sit on the grid, and it is why gradient noise shows no square bias. The interpolation and the smoothing curve are unchanged.
lessons.title: Gradient noise

lessons.intro: One layer of noise gives features at exactly one size, which is why it reads as blobs rather than as anything from the world. Real surfaces have detail at every scale at once — a coastline has bays, and coves inside the bays, and rocks inside the coves. Fractal noise imitates that by adding the same function to itself several times over, each layer half as strong and twice as fine, and it is the single most useful thing in this module.

stages.body: The loop runs once, so this is the previous lesson's noise wearing a new name, and the picture is the same soft blobs. Two details are worth reading now while the loop is trivial. Dividing by the accumulated weight rather than a fixed number keeps the output in the same range however many times the loop runs, so the next three stages are directly comparable. And doubling the coordinate each pass is what makes the next layer finer.
stages.title: One octave

stages.body: One character changed and the surface acquires texture. The large shapes are still exactly where they were — the first octave is unchanged and carries four sevenths of the total — but each is now roughened by a half-strength layer at twice the frequency, and that in turn by a quarter-strength layer at four times. The eye reads the combination as detail rather than as three separate patterns, which is the whole trick. Nothing was added but a bigger number in the loop.
stages.title: Three octaves

stages.body: Six octaves, and the difference from three is far smaller than the difference three made over one. The sixth layer arrives at one thirty-second of the first's strength and thirty-two times its frequency, which on this preview is finer than a pixel and contributes little but cost — four hashed corners per octave, twenty-four of them a pixel by the sixth. Knowing when the next octave stops earning its keep is a judgement the last module of the course is entirely about.
stages.title: Six octaves, and where it stops paying

stages.body: Amplitude falloff is now a parameter, sweeping between 0.2 and 0.7. Low, and the later octaves barely register: the surface goes smooth and rolling, dominated by its first layer. High, and each octave keeps most of its predecessor's strength, so fine detail competes with coarse and the surface turns gritty and restless. The frequency multiplier is the other control, held at two throughout this module; raising it spreads the octaves further apart and starts to look like separate layers rather than one material.
stages.title: The two controls

lessons.takeaway: Summing octaves means adding several passes of noise, each at higher frequency and lower amplitude. Two numbers control the character: how fast frequency rises, and how fast amplitude falls. Halving amplitude while doubling frequency is the usual choice and gives natural-looking detail; keeping more amplitude in the later octaves gives a rougher, grittier surface. Dividing by the total amplitude keeps the output in the same range whatever the octave count.
lessons.title: Fractal noise

lessons.intro: Module 5 spent five lessons transforming coordinates with things you chose: an offset, an angle, a grid. This lesson transforms them with something you did not choose — noise. Feeding a noise field back into the position another noise field is sampled at produces structure that neither could make alone, and it is how most convincing procedural clouds, smoke and marble are actually built. The idea takes one line and repays it generously.

stages.body: Five octaves of fractal noise, unwarped, so the next three stages have something to be compared against. It is a perfectly good cloudy texture and it has one giveaway: everything in it is roughly the same size and roughly round. There are no long thin structures, nothing that looks stretched or swept, because every octave was sampled on a grid that runs straight. That is the specific shortcoming the next stage removes.
stages.title: Before the warp

stages.body: Two more fbm calls build an offset vector, and the field is sampled at the position plus that offset. Every pixel is now reading the texture from somewhere slightly else, and because the offset varies smoothly the whole image looks pushed around — stretched in some places, bunched in others, with the round blobs pulled into curved sweeps. The two offset components are sampled at deliberately different places, so they vary independently rather than dragging everything along one diagonal.
stages.title: Offset the coordinate by noise

stages.body: The same move applied twice: the first offset warps a second offset, which warps the final sample. The result is qualitatively different rather than merely more so — long filaments appear, with fine wisps trailing off them and dense knots where the warp folded the field back on itself. This is the shape people recognise as smoke or marble, and it costs five fractal-noise calls a pixel — twenty-five noise layers, a hundred hashed corners — which is worth knowing before reaching for it in something that has to hold sixty frames a second.
stages.title: Warp the warp

stages.body: Warped noise driving a palette, drifting on time, with the warp vector itself brightening the places it stretched hardest. Every idea in it has a lesson behind it: normalised aspect-corrected coordinates, a cosine palette, a hash, gradient noise, summed octaves, and a coordinate transform — except the transform is noise rather than a matrix. Six modules of machinery, sixteen lines of shader, and nothing in it that has not already been explained.
stages.title: The whole course in one image

lessons.takeaway: Domain warping means offsetting a coordinate by the output of a noise function before sampling noise again. One pass stretches and folds the field into something that looks flowed rather than sprinkled; feeding the result back a second time produces the wispy, filament-like structure associated with smoke and marble. The warp strength is the control worth reaching for first, and past about one unit the image stops being recognisable.
lessons.title: Domain warping

steps.brief: The screen is flat grey. Use the hash to give every cell of a coarse grid its own unrelated value, which should look like television static rather than anything with structure.
steps.hint: floor first, or every pixel gets its own value.
steps.title: Static, one value per cell

steps.brief: Static has no structure because neighbouring cells know nothing about each other. Swap the raw hash for fractal noise so nearby points agree, and the field gains features at several sizes at once.
steps.hint: fbm sums five octaves and normalises the result.
steps.title: Make it continuous

steps.brief: Turn the noise into a surface. Threshold it into patches, use those as a mask between two colours, and warp the coordinate with noise first so the patches stretch rather than staying round.
steps.hint: Sample the two warp components at different places, or everything drags one way.
steps.title: Wear the paint away

modules.description: Assemble independent parts into one deliberate image.

lessons.intro: Six modules have produced parts: shapes, fields, palettes, patterns, noise. None of them said how to put two things in one picture. The answer has been quietly present since Module 4 and is worth stating plainly, because everything else in this module is built on it. A layer is a colour and a mask, applied over whatever is already there, and an image is a stack of those applied in a deliberate order.

stages.body: Three layers, applied in order. A vertical gradient fills the frame, a coral disc goes over it, and a gold bar goes over both. Each layer is the same shape of statement — mix the running colour toward a new one, by a mask — and none of them knows anything about the others. The bar crosses the disc and covers it, because the bar's line runs last. Nothing here is new except the discipline of writing every layer identically.
stages.title: A layer is a colour and a mask

stages.body: The two layer blocks have swapped places and nothing else changed — same disc, same bar, same masks, same colours. Now the coral disc covers the gold bar where they meet, and the bar appears to pass behind it. There is no depth in this shader and no sorting; the later statement simply writes over the earlier one. That is the whole of occlusion here, and it is worth being deliberate about because moving one block silently changes the picture.
stages.title: Order decides what is in front

stages.body: A fourth layer goes on top, and its mask comes from fractal noise rather than from a shape. Nothing about the compositing changed: it is the same mix against the same running colour. Because five-octave noise sits mostly between 0.3 and 0.67, the threshold is set inside that band rather than at a half by habit: roughly the brighter third of the field clears it at all, and only the brightest patches reach full strength. Drifting the coordinate makes the wisps move across the shapes beneath.
stages.title: A layer can be anything that makes a mask

stages.body: Two independent softenings, worth separating in your head. The disc's mask now ramps across a wide band instead of a pixel, so its edge is a long fade rather than a boundary — that is softness. And the whole mask is then scaled by 0.6, so even at its centre the disc only ever reaches six tenths of the way to coral and the gradient behind stays visible through it — that is opacity. The bar keeps a hard edge at full strength for contrast.
stages.title: Masks need not be all or nothing

lessons.takeaway: Compositing is one line repeated: take what you have, mix a new colour over it, and let a mask decide where. Because each layer only reads the accumulated colour, layers stay independent and can be reordered, removed or written in any order you like — but the sequence they run in decides what covers what. A mask is an ordinary number between 0 and 1, so partial and soft coverage cost nothing extra.
lessons.title: Layers and order
lessons.tryThis: In the last stage, raise the disc's opacity from 0.6 to 1.0 while leaving its soft mask alone. It becomes solid in the middle and still fades at the rim, which shows that edge softness and layer opacity are two separate controls.

lessons.intro: Module 3 made the case that a field is worth keeping because it can be read more than one way. This lesson spends that idea properly, with the shape written once as a function and then asked several different questions. It also treats masks as what they are — plain numbers — which means they combine with ordinary arithmetic rather than needing anything new, and can be built from noise or angle just as readily as from a shape.

stages.body: The shape is a rounded box united with a circle overlapping its top edge — Module 3's min, written once as a function. Three masks come out of the single field it returns: a glow that fades over the 0.4 outside it, a fill for everything inside, and an outline for the thin band where the field is near zero. They are composited in that order, so the outline sits over the fill and both sit over the glow. One evaluation, three layers.
stages.title: One field, three questions

stages.body: A mask is a number, so the ordinary arithmetic already means something. Multiplying two masks keeps only where both are high, which is an intersection: the shape's fill times a stripe pattern gives roughly nineteen bands that stop exactly at the shape's edge, because outside it one factor is zero. Subtracting a mask from 1 inverts it, which is how the stripes are tinted rather than punched out. No new function was needed for either.
stages.title: Masks combine like numbers

stages.body: The shape's fill is multiplied by a noise mask, and the intersection wears the shape away in patches — paint flaking off metal. Nothing about the shape changed and nothing about the noise knows a shape exists; the multiplication is the only thing connecting them. This is the argument for keeping masks as plain signals rather than baking them into whatever drew them, because a mask built for one purpose combines with one built for another without either being rewritten.
stages.title: A mask from somewhere else entirely

stages.body: A drop shadow is the same field asked about a different place. Calling scene with the coordinate shifted puts a copy down and to the right, and reading it with a wide smoothstep rather than fwidth makes that copy soft instead of crisp. Composited underneath at just over half strength, it reads as a shadow. Writing the shape as a function is what made this three lines: the alternative is maintaining two copies of a shape and hoping they stay in step.
stages.title: The same function, moved

lessons.takeaway: Write the shape as a function and every treatment becomes a question you ask it: fill inside, outline near zero, glow outside, shadow from the same function sampled at an offset. Masks are numbers between 0 and 1, so multiplying intersects them, taking a max unites them, and subtracting from 1 inverts them. Nothing in this lesson needed a new built-in — only the discipline of naming the field once.
lessons.title: Masks as reusable signals

lessons.intro: This is the last lesson of the first half of the course, and it does not introduce anything. Instead it builds one image from nothing to finished across four stages, adding a single layer at a time and saying why each one earns its place. Every technique in it has a lesson behind it, and the point is to watch a picture assemble the way you would actually write one: background first, subject next, then the things that make it sit together.

stages.body: A vertical gradient from warm at the bottom to deep blue by around five sixths of the way up, then a vignette that dims the frame toward its corners. The vignette is the same radial field from Module 3 used as a multiplier rather than a shape, and it drops the corners to a little under six tenths of full brightness. Neither layer is interesting alone. Both exist so that everything added later has something to sit against.
stages.title: Background first

stages.body: A sun: a circle left of centre and slightly above the middle, with a broad halo taken from the same field before the disc is drawn over it. The halo goes down first at just under half strength so the disc's crisp edge survives on top of it, and both use the warm end of the palette so they belong to the gradient rather than sitting on it. This is Module 2's soft edge and Module 3's glow doing exactly what they did there, in service of something.
stages.title: The subject

stages.body: A horizon, built by sampling fractal noise along one axis and treating the result as a height. Wherever a pixel sits below that height it belongs to the ground, which is the same sign test every field in Module 3 used, applied to a line that happens to wobble. Worth knowing: a single line through two-dimensional noise travels far less than the field does, so the amplitude here is deliberately larger than it looks like it should be. The ridge runs between roughly 0.15 and 0.44 below the centre line, clear of the sun at both ends.
stages.title: Ground the picture

stages.body: Three final layers, none of which announces itself. Haze warms a band hugging the horizon, so the land meets the sky instead of being pasted onto it. Grain adds a hashed value per pixel at three percent, which breaks up the perfectly smooth gradient the way film would. And a contrast nudge around the mid grey from Module 4 firms the whole thing up, clamped because pushing away from a pivot leaves the range at both ends. Compare it against the previous stage.
stages.title: The layers nobody notices

lessons.takeaway: A finished image is usually a short stack of unremarkable layers. Build the background before the subject, and the atmosphere after both, because each layer wants to read against what is already there. The last stage adds nothing anyone would notice individually — haze, grain, a contrast nudge — and the difference between it and the stage before is most of what separates a shader that looks assembled from one that looks placed.
lessons.title: Assembling a finished piece

modules.description: March a ray through space and find where it hits a 3D shape.

lessons.intro: Every shader up to here has answered a question about a point on a flat plane: given this coordinate, what colour? Ray marching asks something different. From an eye somewhere in space, looking out through this pixel, what is there? Answering that needs two vectors per pixel — where the ray starts, and which way it points — and building those is all this lesson does. There is no geometry yet and nothing to hit, so every stage paints the direction itself, which is the only honest way to check a camera before there is a scene to check it against.

stages.body: The first three lines are Module 1's, unchanged, but the preview they run on is a landscape band — between 1.4 and 2.4 times as wide as it is tall, depending on the screen. So p runs minus one to one vertically on every device, while the aspect line pushes it out to at least 1.4 either side horizontally, and further still on a wider screen. The two lines after that are the entire camera: every pixel shares one origin, and each gets its own direction, built by treating the screen coordinate as x and y and bolting 1.5 on as z. normalize scales that to unit length, which is what makes a distance travelled along it mean a distance in the world. Painting z alone shows the rays fanning out: 1.0 dead ahead, 0.832 one unit out in any direction — which is exactly the top and bottom edges — and lower still out toward the left and right, meeting 0.731 travelling straight out to the side edge of the narrowest phone and 0.530 on the widest — the frame's true minimum sits in the corners, lower again, since a corner pulls the ray off-axis on both screen axes at once. ro sits there unread, because nothing yet asks where a ray started.
stages.title: One ray per pixel

stages.body: A unit vector has components between minus one and one, and half-plus-half lifts that into the 0 to 1 a colour needs — x into red, y into green, z into blue. The two screen axes behave quite differently here, because the frame is a landscape band, 1.4 to 2.4 times as wide as it is tall. Green is boxed in: 0.223 at the bottom edge, 0.777 at the top, and it can go no further, because p.y stops at one. Red passes through those same 0.223 and 0.777 one unit out and then keeps going to wherever the device puts the side edges — 0.841 at the right edge of the narrowest phone, 0.924 at the right edge of the widest. Blue is 1.0 dead ahead and 0.916 at the top and bottom edges, sagging further into the corners. What you get is a lavender band with red doing most of the travelling.
stages.title: Paint the direction

stages.body: The 1.5 was never explained, and it is the field of view. A direction with a large z points more nearly straight ahead once normalized, so raising it narrows the cone the camera sees through and lowering it widens it. Here it swings between 0.6 and 2.4 every 12.6 seconds, which is a vertical field of view of 118.1 degrees at the wide end and 45.2 at the narrow, against 67.4 at the 1.5 the rest of the module uses — and the horizontal field is wider again by whatever the preview's aspect happens to be. Watch a point away from the middle rather than the centre. At p of 1.0, 1.0, on the top edge and one unit right of centre, the colour runs from 0.825, 0.825, 0.695 wide open to 0.679, 0.679, 0.931 stopped down, while the centre pixel stays 0.5, 0.5, 1.0 throughout, because the ray straight ahead is the one the lens cannot tilt.
stages.title: The third component is the lens

stages.body: ro finally moves. It traces a circle of radius 3 about the point 3 units ahead, passing through the origin once every 15.7 seconds, and the direction is yawed by the same angle using Module 5's mat2 rotation applied to x and z instead of x and y — so the camera keeps looking at the centre of its own orbit. The centre pixel cycles through 0.5, 0.5, 1.0 then 0.0, 0.5, 0.5 then 0.5, 0.5, 0.0 then 1.0, 0.5, 0.5 at the quarter turns, which is the forward direction swinging all the way round. Change the orbit radius and nothing at all happens on screen. An origin is invisible until a ray hits something, and the next lesson builds the something.
stages.title: Move the camera

lessons.takeaway: A camera is two vectors: an origin every pixel shares, and a direction that differs per pixel. The direction is the screen coordinate with a third component bolted on, and normalize scales it to unit length so that a distance travelled along it is a distance in the world. That third component is the field of view — raise it and the cone narrows, lower it and the cone widens — and the origin changes nothing you can see until there is something in front of it to miss.
lessons.title: Camera and ray setup
lessons.tryThis: Set the focal length in the third stage to a fixed 0.4 and work out the colour at p of 1.0, 1.0 — on the top edge, one unit right of centre — before you look at it. Then change the 3.0 in the last stage's orbit radius and confirm that nothing on screen responds at all.

lessons.intro: Module 3 built a circle out of length(p) minus a radius and never had to mention how many dimensions were involved, because length does not care. That is most of this lesson: hand the same expression a vec3 and it is a sphere. What genuinely changes is the viewing problem. A field defined throughout a volume cannot be shown all at once on a flat screen, so until the next lesson supplies a ray to look along, these stages cut one flat slice through the volume at a time and paint that slice as though it were the whole thing.

stages.body: sdSphere is Module 3's circle with vec2 changed to vec3, and nothing else at all. The source builds a 3D point from the screen coordinate with a z of zero, which cuts the sphere through its equator, so the cross-section is a circle of the full radius 0.45 — forty-five per cent of the way to the top and bottom edges, and nowhere near the left and right, which sit at least 1.4 out even on the narrowest screen. The render is pixel-for-pixel a Module 3 disc, and that is the point: nothing has been gained yet except the knowledge that the formula survives the extra dimension. What has changed is that there is now a whole volume of field the screen is not showing you.
stages.title: One more component

stages.body: Driving the slice's z from time cuts the same sphere at a different depth every frame, and the disc that comes back is the cross-section there. Its radius is 0.45 times the cosine of the driving angle: 0.45 at the equator, 0.390 once the slice reaches z 0.225, 0.270 at z 0.36, and zero at the poles — a pinch to nothing every 4.5 seconds, twice per nine-second cycle. That shrinking is the only evidence on screen that this is a sphere rather than a cylinder, and it is evidence you have to watch accumulate over time rather than read off any single frame.
stages.title: Slide the slice

stages.body: Subtracting a centre before measuring moves the sphere, exactly as it moved the circle two modules ago. The slice stays at z zero now and the sphere is what travels: a small circle of radius 0.1 in x and y every 10.5 seconds, and separately back and forth through the slice by 0.35 every 7.0 seconds. On screen those read as two unrelated effects — the disc slides about, and independently its radius breathes between 0.283 and 0.45. Both are one object moving. That a slide and a resize are indistinguishable in kind here is precisely the ambiguity a single slice cannot resolve, and the reason the next lesson stops slicing.
stages.title: Move the sphere instead

stages.body: map is the name this module and the three that follow use for the function returning the whole scene's distance, and here it is two spheres joined by min — Module 3's union, unchanged by the extra dimension. The two sit 0.44 apart in x and 0.3 apart in z, which is 0.533 in space, closer than the 0.68 sum of their radii, so they genuinely intersect. Watch them trade sizes as the slice sweeps: at z zero the left disc is 0.34 and the right 0.16, at z 0.15 both are 0.305, and at z 0.3 the sizes have swapped. Their centres are 0.44 apart on screen and the two radii sum to more than that at every one of those depths, so the outline stays a single joined shape throughout — they come apart only in a sliver around z minus 0.03, where the right disc has already shrunk under 0.101. It then vanishes altogether for about 46 per cent of the cycle, which is the slice leaving that sphere behind.
stages.title: Two spheres, one field

lessons.takeaway: length(p) minus r is a sphere for exactly the reason it was a circle: length measures distance from the origin in any number of dimensions, and subtracting a radius moves the zero surface out to where the edge should fall. Subtracting a centre first moves the sphere, and min unites two of them into one field. These are Module 3's operators carrying one more component, and the function that returns the whole scene's field is conventionally called map.
lessons.title: A 3D sphere

lessons.intro: A slice shows one depth and has no room for the rest, and no amount of care choosing the depth fixes that. The way out is a different question. Send a ray from the camera through the pixel and ask how far it travels before it meets a surface. Nothing computes that distance directly, but a distance field answers something almost as useful at every point in space — how far you may move from here without hitting anything — and asking that question over and over is the entire algorithm.

stages.body: Four steps, written out rather than hidden inside a function. Each asks map how far the nearest surface is and moves exactly that far, which is safe precisely because nothing can be nearer than the nearest thing. The first step is identical for every pixel — map at the camera is 3 minus 1, so every ray leaps 2.0 — and only after that do they diverge. Painting the distance still remaining shows how far each one got: black across a core of radius 0.426, 0.051 out at the silhouette, 0.1 at radius 0.585, and not reaching white until 0.899. Past that it clips, and on a frame this wide more than half the picture is past that: 1.47 at one unit out, about 3.5 at the side edges on the narrowest phone, and about 7.5 on the widest. Four steps is already most of the way in.
stages.title: Step by the distance you have

stages.body: Sixty-four steps in a loop, with two ways out: the distance dropping below 0.001, which means the ray has arrived, and the total passing 20, which means it never will. The sphere sits 3 units ahead with radius 1, so the tangent ray leaves the camera at asin of one third, 19.47 degrees; multiplying its tangent by the focal length of 1.5 predicts a silhouette of radius 0.530. What renders is 0.533, and since p.y stops at one that is just over half the way to the top and bottom edges — a disc a little over half the frame's height, sitting well clear of the sides on a preview this wide. Every hit falls between t of 2.0 dead ahead and 2.828 at the rim, so 20 is a very generous place to give up.
stages.title: Enough steps, and a test

stages.body: The same scene marched twice, once with the full sixty-four steps and once with twelve, painted so that the disagreement is what you see: cyan where both find the sphere, coral where only the twelve-step march claims to. The coral is a ring from radius 0.533 out to 0.669 — twenty-five per cent too wide, a band 0.135 across in p units wrapped all the way round a disc whose true radius is 0.530. Of the rays that genuinely hit, 85.5 per cent converge inside twelve steps: pixels are area rather than radius, so the figure is the square of the radius ratio and not the ratio itself, and every failure lives in the outer annulus where the steps become tiny. Why the error goes outward rather than inward is the whole of the next lesson.
stages.title: What the extra steps buy

stages.body: Each pixel here is the safe distance at the point its own ray has reached, squashed through d over one plus d so that it stays on screen. float(i) casts the loop counter so it can be compared against a step count that sweeps one to eight and restarts every 7.5 seconds — each count holding 0.83 seconds except the last, which holds 1.67 because the loop's ceiling of eight catches the top of the sweep. A count of zero would be a flat 0.667 everywhere, since map at the camera is 2.0 for every pixel, but the sweep crosses zero in an instant and no frame shows it. Watch the black core spread instead: 0.087, 0.255, 0.362, 0.426, 0.465, 0.489, 0.505, 0.515. One unit out the value dips once and then climbs away, 0.424, 0.405, 0.474, 0.595, 0.729, 0.839, 0.912, 0.954: the second step lands just past that ray's closest approach to the sphere, so it reads lower than the first, and from there every step carries it further out. That brightness is the radius of a ball around the ray guaranteed to be empty, and stepping across it is what gives the technique its other name.
stages.title: Why it is called sphere tracing

lessons.takeaway: map returns the distance to the nearest surface, and that is by definition a distance the ray can travel safely. So march: step that far, resample, step again. The steps shrink as the surface approaches, so the ray converges on it and never passes through, while rays that miss take ever larger steps until they leave — which is why the loop needs a distance at which it gives up as well as a count of tries. More steps buy accuracy at the silhouette and almost nothing anywhere else.
lessons.title: The march loop

lessons.intro: Three numbers went into the last lesson's loop without an argument for any of them: the distance below which it declares a hit, the number of iterations it may spend, and the distance at which it concludes the ray has escaped. None of the three is a property of the sphere. All three are decisions about how much you are willing to spend and how much error you are prepared to accept, and every one of them shows up in the render when it is set wrong. Each stage here moves one of them and measures the damage.

stages.body: The threshold is an argument now, swinging from 0.001 to 0.351 and back every 10.5 seconds. A ray stops as soon as the surface is within it, so what it really stops against is a sphere of radius one plus the threshold, and 1.5 times the tangent of asin of that over 3 predicts a disc growing from 0.531 to 0.757. The render gives 0.533 to 0.749, the shortfall at the loose end being big steps skipping straight past the thin shell. That is forty per cent wider in radius: the disc goes from reaching 53 per cent of the way to the top and bottom edges to reaching 75, on a shape that has not moved and a camera that has not turned.
stages.title: How near counts as a hit

stages.body: Twelve steps, and the loop now says which way it ended: it returns the distance when it converged, and the negation of that distance when it gave up. Painting both readings apart is unkind to the usual test. Cyan marks where the march actually reached the surface, out to radius 0.490. Coral is everything the plain t-under-20 test would have called a hit as well, out to 0.669. The true silhouette is 0.530 and sits inside the coral band — the honest test falls 0.040 short, the loose one runs 0.138 long. Raise the ceiling back to sixty-four and the loose test's error drops to 0.003, which is why the previous lesson got away with it.
stages.title: When the loop runs out

stages.body: The far distance is the one that looks like a background control and is not. It swings between 1.6 and 3.2 here, and because the nearest point of the sphere sits at t of 2.0, anything below 2.0 empties the screen completely — a third of the cycle, about 4.2 seconds of nothing at all. Above it the disc grows back through 0.191 at 2.05, 0.359 at 2.2, 0.463 at 2.4 and 0.514 at 2.6, reaching its full 0.531 at 2.828, which is the distance to the rim. Beyond that it buys nothing: 3.2 gives 0.533. A far distance inside your scene does not trim the background, it removes scene.
stages.title: Where space stops

stages.body: A threshold of 0.3, six steps and a far distance of 2.4, marched alongside a correct sixty-four-step march so that the difference is on screen: cyan where the good one hits, coral where only the broken one does. The coral reaches radius 0.639, twenty per cent too wide — a band 0.106 across in p units laid all the way round the correct silhouette. The worse damage is invisible here. Since map at the camera is 2.0 for every pixel, and the second sample is already under 0.3 anywhere inside radius 0.532, every ray on the face of the sphere returns t of exactly 2.0 — a constant. The depth is gone, which matters because the next lesson reads nothing but t.
stages.title: All three, set badly

lessons.takeaway: The threshold decides how near counts as touching, and because raising it lets grazing rays stop against a wider band of surface, it swells the silhouette rather than softening it. The step ceiling decides how long the loop may creep, and when it runs out the t it returns is neither a hit nor a miss — so a loop that can exhaust should say so rather than let the caller guess from t alone. The far distance decides where space stops, and set too near it cuts the scene instead of the background.
lessons.title: The hit test

lessons.intro: Every march so far has thrown away almost everything it worked out. The loop returns t, the distance the ray travelled before stopping, and each shader has asked exactly one question of it: is that small enough to count as a hit? But t is depth. It says how far away the surface is at this pixel, in the same units the scene itself is built in, and it is already sitting in a variable that cost nothing extra to fill. This lesson spends it four ways, and the first two are worth doing mostly for what they expose.

stages.body: Dividing t by 20 and painting it grey is the naive move, and it is worth watching it fail. The background is pure white, because a ray that escapes returns something at or above 20 and the division cannot bring that under one. The sphere is a near-black disc: 0.100 dead ahead, 0.107 at radius 0.3, 0.126 at 0.5, and 0.139 at the rim. That is the entire shape rendered inside a band 0.039 wide out of a possible 1.0. The depth is real and it is correct — it is simply measured in world units, and nothing about world units maps onto a colour channel.
stages.title: Paint t and see almost nothing

stages.body: Two colours and a smoothstep from 1.2 to 3.7 turn depth into something readable, and the camera slides along z by 0.8 either way so there is a range to read — the first time moving ro has changed a single pixel. At its nearest the sphere is 2.2 away: the disc swells to radius 0.766, three-quarters of the way to the top and bottom edges, and the mix never rises above 0.221, so it reads as the near colour throughout. At its furthest, 3.8, it shrinks to 0.409 and the mix runs 0.705 to 0.999 — the rim lands on the far colour exactly, but the pole only reaches 0.422, 0.429, 0.512, whose red is still more than twice the far colour's 0.18. Across one sphere the effect is far weaker: at the middle position the mix runs 0.242 at the pole, 0.296 halfway out, 0.477 at 88 per cent and 0.720 at the rim, so just over half the swing hides in the outer eighth of the radius.
stages.title: Near and far as colour

stages.body: One comparison turns depth into a one-bit signal, and Module 7 spent a lesson on what one-bit signals are for. Here it composites the sphere over a sky built from the ray direction's y — a gradient spanning only 0.223 at the bottom of the frame to 0.777 at the top, because rd.y never reaches further than that, so its ends read 0.079, 0.132, 0.185 and 0.151, 0.338, 0.445 rather than the two colours in full. Those extremes sit on the vertical centre line: one unit out along the top edge the factor has already fallen to 0.743, and it keeps falling all the way to the corner, so on a frame this wide the bands bow rather than run straight. The disc is flat cyan at radius 0.533 with a hard edge, because a mask carries no shading whatever. What it does carry is a shape sitting over a background the very same rays produced.
stages.title: Depth as a mask

stages.body: Module 4's cosine palette takes any scalar at all, and t is a scalar. With c at 2.0 the depth range across the disc, 2.0 to 2.828, covers 1.66 cycles, and the drifting phase turns the whole thing over every 12.5 seconds. The bands are wildly uneven, and that is the finding rather than a flaw: measured outward from the centre, successive quarter-cycles land at 0, 55.0, 73.8, 85.5, 93.0, 97.5 and 99.6 per cent of the radius. Depth barely changes across the face of a sphere and then changes all at once at the rim, and a palette shows that in a way the grey ramp two stages ago could not.
stages.title: Depth into a palette

lessons.takeaway: t is a depth buffer you already own. Painting it raw is useless, because its range has nothing to do with 0 to 1 and has to be remapped by hand. Even remapped it makes a poor shading cue: on a sphere, depth changes slowly across the face and violently at the rim, so any ramp piles up in the outermost tenth of the radius. Where depth earns its keep is as a mask, and as the scalar behind a palette.
lessons.title: Depth

modules.title: Ray Marching

modules.description: Describe and combine three-dimensional shapes in ray-marched space.

lessons.intro: A sphere is the one solid whose distance function needs no thought, because length already measures it and does not care how many components it was handed. Everything else has to be constructed, and the two shapes here are constructed by quite different tricks. A box comes from folding space with abs so that only one corner of it has to be reasoned about, then measuring how far past that corner you are. A torus comes from taking a distance you have already worked out and using it as a coordinate for a second one. Both are three lines long, both are exact everywhere, and both are still Module 3's operators with one more component along for the ride.

stages.body: abs(p) reflects every octant of space onto the one where all three components are positive, so a box centred on the origin only has to be measured once, in that corner. q is what is left after subtracting the half-extents: how far past the box you are on each axis, negative where you are still inside it. At the box's own centre q is minus 0.6, minus 0.45, minus 0.6; max of that against zero is nothing at all, so the first term contributes nothing, and the second returns minus 0.45, the distance to the nearest face. Step 0.3 beyond one face and q's first component becomes 0.3 while the other two stay negative, so the length is 0.3 and the second term clamps away. Step past two faces at once and q is 0.3, 0.3, minus 0.6, whose positive part has length 0.4243 — the true diagonal distance to the edge, which no single axis could have given. The render is an exact rectangle, because a box seen straight down its own axis is one: 0.6 and 0.45 over the near face's depth of 2.4, times the focal length of 1.5, gives half-extents of 0.375 and 0.28125, and the march reports 0.3756 and 0.2818, the extra thousandth in each being the hit threshold. That is 28.2 per cent of the way to the top and bottom edges, and on a preview between 1.4 and 2.4 times as wide as it is tall it sits well clear of the sides at every width. Every hit lands on the single front face: t runs 2.400 dead ahead and 2.514 at the corners, and all of that spread is the rays fanning out rather than the surface receding.
stages.title: abs folds space into one corner

stages.body: Subtracting a constant from any distance field moves its zero surface outward by that much in every direction at once, and on a box that means the flats move out and the edges become quarter-cylinders. Shrinking the half-extents by the same amount first is what keeps the overall size fixed, so the solid still reaches 0.6, 0.45 and 0.6 whatever r is doing. Here r sweeps from 0 to 0.30 and back every 10.47 seconds, and at the bottom of that sweep the render is the previous stage exactly, since subtracting nothing from a box shrunk by nothing is the box. What the rounding costs is not spread evenly. Straight out sideways the silhouette falls from 0.3756 to 0.3387, 9.82 per cent; straight up it falls from 0.2818 to 0.2537, 9.98 per cent; but measured out along the 45-degree diagonal it falls from 0.3986 to 0.3379, 15.23 per cent. The 0.3986 is worth pausing on: with sharp edges it is exactly the square root of two times the half-height, which is what having a corner there means. At the top of the sweep the flat part of the front face is only 0.6 by 0.3 in world units and everything outside that is fillet, which is why the corner gives up half as much again as the flats do.
stages.title: Subtract a radius

stages.body: length(p.xz) minus the major radius is Module 3's circle, computed in the plane the ring lies in: it says how far you are from the ring's centre line, positive outside and negative inside. That number is not the answer, it is a coordinate. Pair it with p.y and you have a two-dimensional offset from the nearest point of the ring, and the length of that, less the tube radius, is the distance to the surface. Two circles, one nested inside the other. The swizzle q.xzy hands sdTorus the point with its y and z traded, which stands the ring up so its hole faces the camera. With a major radius of 0.8 and a tube of 0.3 at three units out, the render is a true annulus — the same on every traverse, because the ring is symmetric about the view axis — with an outer edge at 0.5611 and an inner edge at 0.2471 in p units. Geometry agrees: the ring's centre line sits at atan of 0.8 over 3, which is 14.931 degrees, and the tube subtends asin of 0.3 over 3.1048, which is 5.545 degrees, so the two edges should fall at 0.5601 and 0.2480. Each is out by about a thousandth, in the direction the hit threshold pushes them, and the solid is fatter on both sides. The hole is genuinely empty: on the axis sdTorus returns 0.8 minus 0.3, a clear half a unit, so the centre ray never converges on anything and leaves past 20. The outer edge reaches 56.1 per cent of the way to the top and bottom edges.
stages.title: A distance from a distance

stages.body: min over two fields is the union, and it does not care that the fields describe different kinds of shape or that one lies inside the other's hole. The bar is a box with half-extents of 0.2, 0.2 and 1.0, so it runs from z of 2 to z of 4 and passes clean through the ring. A flat fill would not be able to say which of them is in front, so this stage spends t instead, mixing between the two colours across a smoothstep from 2.0 to 4.0. The bar's near face sits at 2.0, and 1.5 times 0.2 over 2.0 puts its silhouette at exactly 0.15 in p units with corners at 0.2121; the march gives 0.1508 and 0.2129. Those corners reach 0.2828 in world units across the ring's plane, against a hole 0.5 wide, so the two solids never touch — and background shows all the way round between them, a band 0.0961 wide in p units straight out along the two screen axes, narrowing to 0.0338 out at 45 degrees where the bar's corners come nearest the ring's inner edge. The colours say the rest. The bar's front face is flat, running from t of 2.000 to 2.020 across its whole width, so it comes back at very nearly the undiluted near colour, 0.780, 0.960, 0.390. The ring is further and reads it. At the nose of its tube t is 2.805 and the colour 0.567, 0.768, 0.447. Both rims are further than that and identical to each other, which is forced rather than lucky: the silhouette ray on the inside of the ring and the one on the outside are tangent to the same circular cross-section of the tube, and the two tangent lengths from a point to a circle are equal, so each of them sits at a t of 3.0903 and a colour of 0.439, 0.654, 0.481. That is a limit approached rather than reached, since a ray exactly on a tangent grazes for ever, so the outermost pixels that do converge stop short of it on either side, neither of them arriving.
stages.title: Both, with min

lessons.takeaway: abs folds all eight octants onto one, so a box need only be measured in a single corner. q is how far past the box you are on each axis; length(max(q, 0.0)) is the exact distance for a point outside, since the negative components are flattened to zero and drop out of the length, and min(max(q.x, max(q.y, q.z)), 0.0) supplies the inside distance the first term cannot, because inside every component of q is negative and the largest of them names the nearest face. sdTorus is a distance built from a distance: length(p.xz) minus the major radius says how far you are from the ring's circle, and that pairs with p.y into a two-dimensional offset whose length, less the tube radius, is the answer. min unites two of them, unchanged from Module 3.
lessons.title: Box and torus SDFs
lessons.tryThis: Raise the torus's tube radius in the third stage from 0.3 to 0.8, the same as its major radius, and work out what becomes of the hole before you look at it. Then swap min for max in the last stage and say why the picture goes entirely dark, with not one lit pixel left.

lessons.intro: min is the correct answer to a question slightly narrower than the one being asked. It returns the distance to whichever surface is nearer, which is exactly what a union needs and exactly why a union built from min has a hard corner wherever the two surfaces cross: at that crossing the field stops following one shape and starts following the other in an instant, and a field with a kink in it has a kink on its zero surface too. A smooth minimum is min with that switch smeared out over a width you choose. It is one clamp, one mix and one correction term, and past a certain width it does something min can never do.

stages.body: Two spheres of radius 0.5, centred 0.44 either side of the axis and three units out. Their centres are 0.88 apart and their radii sum to 1.0, so they overlap, and the circle where the two surfaces cross has a radius of 0.2375 in world units. min unites them into one solid, and the outline shows precisely where the union was welded and where it was not. The two ends are untouched: the silhouette reaches 0.4841 in p units either side, and the tallest point of each lobe is 0.2550, out at p.x of 0.2263. On the vertical centre line, though, the outline pinches to 0.1220 — 47.9 per cent of the lobe height — and it does not curve into that pinch, it turns a corner. Projecting the intersection circle puts that corner at 0.1191, and the 0.0029 of difference is the hit threshold, which costs more at a corner than anywhere else: a ray creeping past a sharp edge stays within a thousandth of it for a stretch rather than an instant. Tighten the threshold from 0.001 to 0.00001 and the rendered waist walks back to 0.11913, against the 0.11912 the geometry asks for. The corner is not only in the outline. It runs across the surface as a ridge from the top notch to the bottom one; the outline is that same ridge seen edge-on, which is the only part of it a flat fill can show.
stages.title: The corner min leaves

stages.body: The same two spheres, with min replaced by smin at a k of 0.3, and the corner is gone. The waist rises from 0.1220 to 0.1890 in p units, and nothing else on screen moves: the ends stand at 0.484140 with min and 0.484150 with the blend, a difference of one hundred-thousandth, and the tallest point of each lobe stays at 0.2550. That is not luck, it is the clamp. At the right-hand end the near sphere's distance is 0 and the far one's is 0.88; 0.88 is far more than k, so h pins to one end of its range, the correction term collapses to nothing, and smin returns exactly what min returned. The blend can only act where the two distances are within k of each other. Where they are equal it acts hardest, because k times h times one minus h is largest at h of a half, giving k over 4 — here 0.075. So on the vertical centre line the field reads 0.075 less than it did, and the surface moves out to where the old field was 0.075: solving that puts the waist's world half-height at 0.3702 instead of 0.2375. At three units out the camera turns one world unit into half a unit of p, so that 0.1327 of world becomes 0.0663 on screen — against the 0.0670 the render actually moves, the remainder being the same threshold that widened the corner in the last stage.
stages.title: smin welds it

stages.body: k is an argument now, sweeping from 0.02 to 0.50 and back every 12.57 seconds, and what it moves is worth watching against what it leaves alone. The waist climbs steadily: 0.1272 at the bottom of the sweep, 0.1465 at k of 0.10, 0.1685 at 0.20, 0.1890 at 0.30, 0.2083 at 0.40 and 0.2269 at the top, against 0.1220 for the plain min of the first stage. Over the whole sweep the two ends move from 0.484140 to 0.484155 and the lobes stay 0.2550 tall to four decimal places. The entire effect is confined to the join, and the reason is arithmetic rather than taste: away from the join the two distances differ by much more than k, h saturates, and smin is min. Note that k is not a screen measurement. It is a world distance, and at this depth the camera turns one world unit into half a unit of p. What the blend spends is not k either but k over 4, the height of the correction term: at the top of the sweep that is 0.125 of world, whose straight projection would be 0.0625 of p, and yet the waist has risen 0.1049 above where min left it. A surface moves by its field's drop divided by how steeply that field was climbing, and between two nearly opposed surfaces it climbs slowly, so the same drop buys more travel there than it would anywhere else.
stages.title: k is the control

stages.body: These two spheres do not touch. Radius 0.42, centred 0.5 either side of the axis, so their surfaces face each other across a gap of 0.16 and no amount of min will ever join them: min would give two discs for ever, with inner edges at plus and minus 0.0399 by geometry and 0.0388 as rendered, leaving a strip of background 0.0775 wide down the middle. smin can join them, and exactly when it does is predictable. At the midpoint both distances are 0.08, which is the case where smin returns the distance minus k over 4, so the field there is 0.08 minus a quarter of k and it reaches zero at k of 0.32 precisely. Below that the strip merely narrows — 0.0388 of p either side of the axis at a k of 0.05, still 0.0131 at 0.30 — and above it there is a weld, reaching 0.0262 above the axis right at the threshold, 0.0765 at k of 0.40, 0.1124 at 0.50 and 0.1407 at 0.60. k sweeps 0.05 to 0.60 every 12.57 seconds, so by the arithmetic the two are one shape for 6.36 of those seconds and two for the rest. What gets drawn runs longer, and not merely because a field within 0.001 of zero counts as solid. Near the onset the field along the axis is so nearly flat that the march spends all sixty-four of its steps without ever converging, and since the t it hands back is still under 20, the fill paints it solid anyway. That lights the middle of the frame at a k of 0.3082 on the narrowest preview and the widest alike, stretching the joined part of the cycle to 6.53 seconds; a preview an odd number of pixels across sits its columns half a pixel over, lights at 0.3095, and gets 6.51. Through all of it the lobes are untouched, reaching 0.4714 either side and 0.2133 above and below at every k in the sweep.
stages.title: A shape that needs the blend

lessons.takeaway: smin interpolates between the two distances rather than picking one. h is where the two stand relative to each other, scaled by k and clamped, so once they differ by more than k it saturates and smin returns exactly what min would — which is why blending never disturbs the parts of a shape away from the join. The correction term k times h times one minus h peaks at a quarter of k in the middle, so where the two distances are equal the field is pushed down by k over 4 and the surface moves outward to meet the new zero. k is measured in world units, not screen units, and a k large enough will weld together two shapes that never touch at all.
lessons.title: Smooth minimum
lessons.tryThis: In the third stage, work out from the field alone how far the waist should sit above the sphere centres when k is 0.5, then check it against what renders. In the last stage, move the spheres to plus and minus 0.6 and predict the new k at which the weld appears before you change anything else.

lessons.intro: Every scene so far has held as many shapes as its map function had lines. Repetition breaks that relationship. Take the point the ray has reached, keep only where it sits inside a cell of a grid, and hand that to a single sphere: the same three lines now describe a lattice running away for ever in all three directions, and it costs what one sphere cost. Module 5 did this on a flat plane with a shape that was drawn rather than marched, so a wrong answer merely looked odd. Here the same arithmetic feeds a loop that trusts every number it is given, and the first stage is what that trust buys when the arithmetic is careless.

stages.body: fract runs 0 to 1 on each axis, so the point handed to sdSphere is measured from the low corner of whichever cell the ray is in, and a sphere written around the origin therefore sits on that corner. Only the eighth of it with all three components positive is inside the cell, so what this field actually describes is an eighth-sphere at every whole-numbered point in space. The geometry is the smaller of the two problems. Cross a cell wall and fract falls from just under one to zero, which drops the reported distance from as much as 1.4321 to minus 0.3 across no distance at all. That is not a distance field, it is a function that happens to be zero on a surface, and the march believes it: a ray told it may safely travel 1.4321 travels 1.4321, straight through whatever was 0.001 ahead. Counted pixel by pixel when the camera passes a whole-numbered depth, the narrowest preview reports 30.07 per cent of the frame stopping inside the solid against 1.19 per cent that reaches an actual surface, with 68.58 per cent walking through everything and leaving; the widest preview gives 29.34, 3.36 and 67.02. What is on screen is that arithmetic: fragments and speckle where a whole lattice should be. The camera runs down the line x equals y equals 0.5, half a cell from the lumps in both screen axes, because the origin itself is inside one of them.
stages.title: fract, and what it costs

stages.body: One term fixes both faults. fract(p) minus 0.5 runs from minus a half to a half, so the sphere sits in the middle of its cell and no longer needs cutting up, and the value no longer jumps: crossing a wall swings the coordinate from just under a half to just over minus a half, which is a sign change in a quantity whose length is what matters. For a sphere the result is not an approximation, it is exact.
